chapters.title: Introduction & How to Approach System Design
chapters.summary: Foundation chapter covering what system design is, interview types, the 6-step delivery framework, back-of-the-envelope estimation, and the numbers every engineer must memorize.

explanation.overview: System design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data flow of a system to satisfy specified requirements. In interviews, you're evaluated on your ability to break down ambiguous problems, make well-reasoned trade-off decisions, and communicate clearly. There is no single right answer — the process and reasoning matter more than the final diagram.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: A system design interview typically runs 45-60 minutes. The interviewer starts with an open-ended prompt like 'Design Twitter' or 'Design a distributed rate limiter'. You must drive the conversation — the interviewer acts as a product manager you're collaborating with. You are scored on four axes: (1) Problem Exploration — did you ask the right clarifying questions and scope the problem correctly? (2) Technical Breadth — can you draw a complete, coherent high-level architecture? (3) Technical Depth — can you dive deep into 2-3 components and discuss internals, edge cases, trade-offs? (4) Communication — did you structure your thoughts, explain trade-offs, and adapt to interviewer signals?

children.title: What is System Design?
children.summary: System design is the art of defining how software components interact to fulfil functional and non-functional requirements at scale.

explanation.overview: System design sits at the intersection of software engineering and infrastructure engineering. You decompose a large problem into smaller components (services, databases, caches, queues), define clear interfaces between them (REST APIs, event contracts), choose the right technologies for each component, and reason about how the system behaves under load, failure, and growth.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Internally, every large-scale system follows the same fundamental pattern: requests arrive from clients, pass through layers of routing and processing, interact with storage systems, and return responses. The challenge is making this work for millions of users simultaneously while keeping latency low, availability high, data consistent, and costs reasonable. The design process is about finding the right balance between these competing forces.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: What the system must DO. These are user-facing features. Examples: 'Users can post tweets up to 280 characters', 'Users can follow other users', 'Users can view a chronological feed of posts from people they follow'. Each FR drives at least one API endpoint and one data flow in your architecture. Always enumerate exactly 3-5 FRs during an interview — too few means you missed scope, too many means you'll run out of time.

HOW the system must behave. These are quality attributes. Key NFRs to always consider: Availability (what SLA? 99.9% = 8.7 hrs downtime/year), Latency (p99 target? < 200ms for user-facing), Scalability (how many users/requests? 100M DAU?), Consistency (strong or eventual? financial = strong, social feed = eventual), Durability (can we lose data? payments = never, logs = acceptable), Security (PCI compliance? E2E encryption?). Pick the top 2-3 most critical NFRs and state them explicitly.

A box-and-arrow architecture diagram showing major components and data flow between them. Typical boxes: Client, CDN, Load Balancer, API Gateway, Application Servers, Cache (Redis), Database (Postgres/Cassandra), Message Queue (Kafka), Worker Services, Blob Storage (S3). Each arrow should be labelled with the protocol/API call. The HLD must satisfy every functional requirement — trace each FR through the diagram.

Detailed design of a single component: class diagrams, database schemas, specific algorithm choices, API request/response formats, state machines. In an SD interview, LLD shows up in deep dives — for example, designing the exact database schema for a URL shortener, or the leader-election algorithm in a distributed cache. In dedicated LLD interviews, you design the internals of a single system like a parking lot or elevator.

Every design decision involves trade-offs. The hallmark of a strong candidate is explicitly stating trade-offs rather than just picking a technology. Example: 'I'm choosing Cassandra over PostgreSQL because we have a write-heavy workload (500K writes/sec). The trade-off is we lose JOIN support and strong consistency, but our access patterns don't require joins and eventual consistency is acceptable for a social feed.' Always use the pattern: 'I chose X because [reason]. The trade-off is [downside], which is acceptable because [justification].'

FAANG 2024 Trend: A document that captures an important architectural decision made along with its context and consequences. In an interview, treating the whiteboard like an ADR proves seniority. Structure: Context (why are we making this choice?), Options (what did we consider?), Decision (what did we choose?), Consequences (what are the trade-offs we accepted?).

examples.title: FR/NFR Scoping Example — Design Twitter
examples.description: Functional Requirements: (1) Users can post tweets (text, up to 280 chars, optionally with images). (2) Users can follow/unfollow other users. (3) Users can view their home timeline — a feed of recent tweets from people they follow, in reverse chronological order. Non-Functional Requirements: (1) Highly available — 99.99% uptime (< 52 min downtime/year). (2) Read-heavy — 10:1 read:write ratio (most users browse, few post). (3) Low latency — feed loads in < 200ms p99. (4) Eventual consistency is acceptable — a new tweet can take up to 5 seconds to appear in followers' feeds. (5) Scale target: 500M users, 200M DAU, ~10K tweets/sec average.

examples.title: Java: Defining the Core API Interface Before Architecture
examples.description: In senior interviews, writing a clean interface before drawing boxes proves you understand the contract boundaries.

examples.title: Python (FastAPI): Mocking the Read Path (Timeline)
examples.description: Using standard Python typing to demonstrate cursor-based pagination for feeds.
examples.code:
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends, Query
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import List, Optional
import uuid

class TweetResponse(BaseModel):
    tweet_id: uuid.UUID
    content: str
    timestamp: int

class FeedResponse(BaseModel):
    tweets: List[TweetResponse]
    next_cursor: Optional[str]

router = APIRouter()

@router.get('/api/v1/feed', response_model=FeedResponse)
async def get_timeline(
    user_id: uuid.UUID,
    cursor: Optional[str] = Query(None, description="Base64 encoded timestamp+id for pagination"),
    limit: int = Query(20, le=100)
):
    # Returning the abstract contract
    pass

common_mistakes: Not asking clarifying questions and assuming scope — always confirm: mobile vs web? global or single region? real-time or batch?
Listing too many functional requirements (>5) — you won't have time. Focus on the core features that drive the architecture.
Ignoring non-functional requirements — scale/latency targets fundamentally change the architecture (a system for 1K users is completely different from one for 100M users).
Jumping to technology choices before understanding requirements — 'let's use Kafka!' without knowing if you need async processing.

configurable_params.name: Library Configuration Parameters
configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Tuning configuration to drop stale packets reduces latency but requires robust frontend exception handling.

children.title: Types of System Design Interviews
children.summary: Three main types of system design interviews, each requiring different focus areas and evaluation criteria.

explanation.overview: Not all system design interviews are the same. The type determines what the interviewer focuses on and what signals they're looking for.

key_concepts.definition: The most common type. You design a user-facing product like Twitter, Uber, WhatsApp, or Instagram. Focus areas: (1) Understanding user flows and translating them into API endpoints. (2) Designing data models that support the access patterns. (3) Choosing the right storage (SQL vs NoSQL) based on data relationships and scale. (4) Fan-out strategies for feeds and notifications. (5) Real-time features (WebSockets for chat, SSE for live comments). The interviewer evaluates whether your architecture correctly implements all FRs and handles the stated scale. Edge cases: celebrity problem (user with 100M followers), hot partitions, thundering herds.

You design a foundational building block used by other systems: a distributed rate limiter, distributed cache, job scheduler, key-value store, or message queue. Focus areas: (1) Distributed systems fundamentals — consensus, replication, partitioning. (2) Failure handling — what happens when a node crashes? Network partition? (3) Consistency guarantees — is this CP or AP? (4) Internal algorithms — hash ring for consistent hashing, skip lists for sorted sets, LSM trees for write-heavy stores. The interviewer goes much deeper on internals here. They expect you to discuss Raft/Paxos, quorum reads/writes, and failure modes.

You design a system that involves machine learning: recommendation engine, ad ranking, spam detection, search ranking. Focus areas: (1) Data pipeline — how do you collect, clean, and store training data? (2) Feature engineering — what signals predict the outcome? (3) Model architecture — collaborative filtering, two-tower model, transformer. (4) Model serving — online inference latency, batching, GPU allocation. (5) A/B testing and feedback loops. The interviewer evaluates whether you understand the end-to-end ML lifecycle, not just the model.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: If the prompt is ambiguous, e.g., 'Design a search system'
advanced_tweaks.how: Ask: 'Would you like me to focus on the user-facing product design (search UI, ranking, suggestions) or the infrastructure side (building the inverted index, distributed crawling, query parsing)?' This shows maturity and lets the interviewer steer you toward what they're evaluating.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: Always
advanced_tweaks.how: Product SD: spend 60% on HLD and API design. Infrastructure SD: spend 60% on deep dives and internals. ML SD: spend time on data pipeline and model serving, not just the model itself.

children.title: Interview Delivery Framework (6 Steps)
children.summary: A battle-tested 6-step structure to deliver a system design interview within 45 minutes, ensuring you cover requirements, API, architecture, and deep dives.

explanation.overview: This framework provides a repeatable structure so you never freeze or wander aimlessly. It forces you to move from abstract (requirements) to concrete (architecture), then zoom into the hardest parts (deep dives). The specific time allocations are guidelines — adapt based on interview length and interviewer signals.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: The framework mirrors how senior engineers actually design systems in industry: start with a problem statement (PRD), define requirements, scope an MVP, design the architecture, then iterate on bottlenecks. The interview compresses weeks of work into 45 minutes, so you must be ruthlessly efficient.

step_by_step.title: Clarify Requirements (~5 min)
step_by_step.detail: This is the most underrated step. Bad candidates skip it and jump into drawing boxes. Great candidates ask precise questions that reveal hidden complexity. Questions to ask: 'What is the expected scale? DAU? Reads vs writes ratio?' 'Do we need real-time updates or is eventual consistency OK?' 'What's the geographic distribution? Single region or global?' 'What are the SLA targets? Availability? Latency p99?' 'Are there any hard constraints — regulatory (GDPR), compliance (PCI), cost budget?' EDGE CASE: If the interviewer says 'you decide', make a reasonable assumption, state it explicitly ('I'll assume 100M DAU, read-heavy 10:1'), and move on. This shows you can make decisions under ambiguity. OUTPUT: Write down ~3-5 functional requirements and ~2-3 non-functional requirements on the whiteboard/doc.

step_by_step.title: Core Entities (~2 min)
step_by_step.detail: Extract the core nouns from your requirements. These become your database tables or document collections. Example for Twitter: User, Tweet, Follow (relationship), Timeline, Media. Keep it simple — 4-6 entities max. Don't design the full schema yet, just list the entities. This step grounds the conversation before you start drawing architecture boxes.

step_by_step.title: API Design (~5 min)
step_by_step.detail: Define the key API endpoints that implement your functional requirements. Use REST or describe event interfaces for async systems. For each endpoint: HTTP method, path, request body, response body, status codes. Example: POST /api/v1/tweets — body: {user_id, content, media_ids[]} — response: 201 {tweet_id, created_at}. GET /api/v1/feed?user_id=X&cursor=abc&limit=20 — response: 200 {tweets[], next_cursor}. INDUSTRY TWEAK: Always use cursor-based pagination (not offset) — offsets break when new items are inserted. EDGE CASE: For write-heavy systems (payments), include an idempotency_key header to prevent duplicate processing on retries.

step_by_step.title: [Optional] Data Flow (~5 min)
step_by_step.detail: For pipeline or data-processing systems (web crawler, ad click aggregator, metrics monitoring), trace the data journey: Ingestion → Processing → Storage → Serving. This replaces or supplements the API step because these systems are event-driven rather than request-driven. Example for Ad Click Aggregator: Click event → Kafka topic → Flink stream processor (aggregate by ad_id + time window) → write aggregated counts to OLAP DB (ClickHouse) → query API reads from OLAP DB.

step_by_step.title: High-Level Design (~10-15 min)
step_by_step.detail: This is the main event. Draw the architecture box-by-box, satisfying each functional requirement. Standard components to consider: DNS → CDN (static assets, edge caching) → Load Balancer (L7, health checks) → API Gateway (auth, rate limiting, routing) → Application Servers (stateless, horizontally scaled) → Cache (Redis — for hot reads, sessions, rate limit counters) → Primary Database (Postgres for relational, Cassandra for write-heavy) → Blob Storage (S3 for media, files) → Message Queue (Kafka for async processing, event streaming) → Worker Services (background jobs, notifications, email). For each FR, trace the flow through the diagram: 'When a user posts a tweet, the request hits the LB → API Server → writes to Postgres → publishes event to Kafka → Fan-out workers consume the event and push the tweet to each follower's cached timeline in Redis.' INDUSTRY STANDARD: Make services stateless. Store all state in databases/caches. This enables horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys.

step_by_step.title: Deep Dives (~10 min)
step_by_step.detail: Pick 2-3 areas that are most interesting, most challenging, or that the interviewer hints at. Use the Bad → Good → Great pattern to show trade-off reasoning. Examples of deep dives: (1) 'How do we handle the celebrity problem in feed generation?' Bad: fan-out on write to all 100M followers → massive write amplification. Good: fan-out on write for normal users, fan-out on read for celebrities (hybrid approach). Great: hybrid + pre-computed celebrity feeds cached at CDN edge. (2) 'How do we ensure exactly-once payment processing?' Bad: retry without dedup → double charges. Good: idempotency key stored in DB → reject duplicate requests. Great: idempotency key + transactional outbox pattern → guarantee event published if payment succeeds. EDGE CASES to discuss in deep dives: What happens during network partitions? What if a database node goes down mid-write? How do we handle a sudden 10× traffic spike (viral event)? What if the cache goes down (thundering herd)?

configurable_params.name: Interview duration
configurable_params.effect: Shorter interviews (35 min) → compress requirements to 3 min, HLD to 10 min, 1 deep dive. Longer (60 min) → can do 3-4 deep dives.
configurable_params.tradeoff: More time on HLD means more complete architecture but less impressive depth. Senior/Staff interviewers care more about depth.

configurable_params.name: Number of FRs
configurable_params.effect: Fewer FRs means simpler HLD and more time for depth. More FRs means broader system but shallow treatment.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Always confirm with interviewer: 'I've identified these 4 requirements — shall I add more or is this the right scope?'

configurable_params.name: Number of deep dives
configurable_params.effect: Each deep dive takes 3-5 minutes. Going deep on one topic is better than shallow on four.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Let the interviewer guide which deep dive matters most — if they keep asking about consistency, dive into consensus.

advanced_tweaks.technique: Lead with the hardest problem (architectural driver)
advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When one requirement dominates the architecture
advanced_tweaks.how: In Google Docs, the core challenge is real-time collaborative editing with conflict resolution. Lead with CRDT/OT in your HLD rather than treating it as a deep dive. This shows you immediately see what makes this problem hard.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: Every deep dive
advanced_tweaks.how: Present a naive solution (polling every 1 second), explain why it fails at scale (1M clients × 1 req/sec = 1M QPS), propose a better approach (long polling — fewer requests), then the best approach (WebSocket — persistent connection, server-pushed updates, ~10K connections per server). This demonstrates trade-off reasoning, which is the #1 signal interviewers look for.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: During HLD and deep dives
advanced_tweaks.how: For every component, briefly mention: 'If the cache goes down, we fall back to the DB with increased latency. We'd also see a cache stampede — to mitigate, we use mutex-based single-flight cache population.' This shows you think about production reality, not just happy path.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: During HLD step
advanced_tweaks.how: Sketch the boxes and arrows first (takes 1-2 minutes), THEN walk through it. This is faster than explaining while drawing and produces a cleaner diagram. Label every arrow with the protocol (HTTP, gRPC, async/Kafka).

common_mistakes: Spending 15+ minutes on requirements — implies you can't scope problems efficiently.
Drawing a monolithic architecture first and then 'adding microservices' — start with a reasonable modular design.
Not labelling arrows — arrows without labels (HTTP? gRPC? async Kafka event?) are meaningless.
Ignoring interviewer hints — if they ask 'what happens when X fails?' three times, that IS the deep dive they want.
Using technologies you can't explain — if you put Kafka in the diagram, you must be able to discuss partitions, consumer groups, and offset management.
Designing for 100M users when the requirement is 100 users — always let NFRs drive complexity.

interview_tips.q: What if the interviewer interrupts and redirects?
interview_tips.a: This is a GOOD sign. It means they've seen enough of your current section and want to explore a specific area. Follow their lead — they know what they're evaluating. Say: 'Great question, let me dive into that.' Don't resist or say 'I'll get to that later.'

interview_tips.q: What if I don't know a specific technology?
interview_tips.a: Describe what you NEED (a distributed log that preserves ordering, supports consumer groups, and handles 100K events/sec) rather than naming a technology. If pressed, say: 'I'd use a system like Kafka or Pulsar for this — the key properties I need are ordered partitions and consumer group semantics.' This shows you understand the requirements even if you can't name every product.

interview_tips.q: Should I write code during system design?
interview_tips.a: Rarely. Only if the interviewer asks, or if a specific algorithm (consistent hashing, LRU cache) is the core of the problem. Most interviewers want architecture diagrams and verbal explanations, not code.

limitations: Over-indexing on Frameworks: Interviewers are explicitly trained to break candidates out of memorized frameworks. If you sound like a robot reading a checklist, they will interrupt you.
Time Misallocation: The biggest failure reason in senior interviews is spending 25 minutes on API definitions and not reaching the complex distributed systems deep dives.
Ignoring the Interviewer: If the interviewer asks about database partitioning in minute 5, abandon the framework and talk about database partitioning. They hold the rubric.

children.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
children.summary: Quick math techniques to estimate QPS, storage, bandwidth, and memory requirements for any system within 2-3 minutes.

explanation.overview: Capacity estimation proves your design is grounded in reality. Rather than guessing, you derive technical requirements from business numbers. Interviewers expect rough order-of-magnitude accuracy (within 2-5×), not exact precision.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: The process always starts from a business metric (DAU, monthly uploads, messages/day) and converts it to infrastructure metrics (QPS, storage/year, bandwidth, server count). You then use these numbers to justify architectural decisions: 'We need 50K QPS reads — a single Postgres instance handles ~10K QPS, so we need read replicas or a cache layer.'

step_by_step.title: Estimate QPS from DAU
step_by_step.detail: QPS = DAU × actions_per_user_per_day ÷ 86,400 seconds. Round 86,400 to ~100,000 for quick math. Peak QPS = 2× to 5× average (use 3× as default). EXAMPLE: Twitter — 200M DAU, each user reads ~100 tweets/day and writes ~0.5 tweets/day. Read QPS = 200M × 100 / 100,000 = 200,000 QPS average → 600K peak. Write QPS = 200M × 0.5 / 100,000 = 1,000 QPS average → 3K peak. INSIGHT: This is a 200:1 read-heavy system → caching and read replicas are critical; write bottleneck is not the main concern.

step_by_step.title: Estimate Storage
step_by_step.detail: Storage/year = writes_per_day × object_size × 365 × replication_factor. First estimate object size: a tweet = tweet_id (8B) + user_id (8B) + content (280 chars = 560B with UTF-16) + timestamp (8B) + metadata (100B) ≈ 700 bytes, round to 1 KB. Storage = 100M tweets/day × 1 KB × 365 = 36.5 TB/year × 3 replicas = ~110 TB/year. Add blob storage separately: if 10% of tweets have images (~500 KB each) → 10M × 500 KB = 5 TB/day = 1.8 PB/year. INSIGHT: Media storage dominates by 10×. Use a separate blob store (S3) for media — never store blobs in your relational database.

step_by_step.title: Estimate Bandwidth
step_by_step.detail: Incoming bandwidth = write_QPS × avg_write_size. Outgoing bandwidth = read_QPS × avg_response_size. EXAMPLE: Read bandwidth = 200K QPS × 10 KB (response with 20 tweets) = 2 GB/s ≈ 16 Gbps outbound. Write bandwidth = 1K QPS × 1 KB = 1 MB/s (negligible). INSIGHT: 16 Gbps outbound is significant — use a CDN to serve media and cache hot feeds at the edge. A single server with 10 Gbps NIC handles ~1.25 GB/s, so you'd need ~2 servers just for network bandwidth, but with CDN offload this drops dramatically.

step_by_step.title: Estimate Cache Size (80/20 Rule)
step_by_step.detail: Cache the top 20% hottest data. Daily unique reads = read_QPS × 86,400 (but with Zipf distribution, ~20% of items serve 80% of reads). Cache size = 0.2 × total_daily_unique_items × item_size. EXAMPLE: 200M unique feed requests/day, each feed = 10 KB. Cache = 0.2 × 200M × 10 KB = 400 GB. A single Redis instance handles ~25-100 GB of RAM → need Redis Cluster with 4-16 shards. EDGE CASE: Hot items (viral tweets) may need extra replication across cache nodes to avoid single-node hotspots.

step_by_step.title: Estimate Server Count
step_by_step.detail: Servers = peak_QPS ÷ QPS_per_server. A typical web server handles 1K-10K QPS depending on workload (CPU-heavy vs I/O-heavy). EXAMPLE: 600K peak QPS ÷ 5K QPS/server = 120 application servers. Add 50% headroom = ~180 servers. INSIGHT: Cloud auto-scaling handles this dynamically — you don't provision all 180 at once. Set min=50, desired=120, max=250 with CPU-based auto-scaling.

key_concepts.definition: In estimation, you care about whether something is 100 GB or 100 TB, not whether it's 87 GB or 113 GB. Being within 2-5× is 'accurate enough' for system design.
In most systems, a small fraction of items receive a disproportionate share of traffic. The most popular 1% of URLs get 90% of hits. This justifies caching — a small cache has a high hit rate.
Multiply storage by the number of copies: typically 3 for databases (primary + 2 replicas), 3 for Kafka, 3 for HDFS. This is for durability — losing one copy doesn't lose data.

examples.title: Full Estimation: Design a URL Shortener
examples.description: Assumptions: 100M new URLs/month, 10:1 read:write ratio (1B reads/month), URLs stored for 5 years, each record ~500 bytes. Write QPS: 100M / (30 × 86,400) ≈ 40 QPS (low — no scaling concern for writes). Read QPS: 1B / (30 × 86,400) ≈ 400 QPS average → 1,200 QPS peak (single server can handle this). Total storage: 100M URLs/month × 12 months × 5 years × 500 bytes × 3 replicas = 100M × 60 × 500 × 3 = 90 TB over 5 years. Cache: top 20% of daily reads × URL record size. 1B reads/month = ~33M/day. Cache 20% = 6.6M × 500B = ~3.3 GB → easily fits in a single Redis instance. Conclusion: This is a small-scale system. Single server + single DB + small Redis cache. The hard problem isn't scale — it's ensuring unique short URLs.

common_mistakes: Over-engineering a small system — if estimation shows 40 QPS, you don't need Kafka, Kubernetes, and a distributed cache. A single server with Postgres is fine.
Forgetting replication factor — raw storage × 3 is a big difference (30 TB vs 90 TB).
Using exact numbers — don't waste time computing 87,329 QPS. Round to 90K. Precision is not the goal.
Not using the estimates — if you calculate 600K QPS and then draw a single database with no caching, your design contradicts your own math.

children.title: Numbers Every Engineer Must Know
children.summary: Essential latency and throughput numbers that help you quickly evaluate whether a design is feasible without benchmarking.

explanation.overview: These numbers (originally from Jeff Dean at Google) give you an intuitive sense of how fast different operations are. When someone proposes 'just read from disk on every request', you instantly know that's ~10ms per read (HDD) and can't sustain 50K QPS on a single server. These numbers don't change much over time — orders of magnitude stay stable even as hardware improves.

key_concepts.definition: ~1 ns. This is the fastest memory access — data already in the CPU's closest cache. Your hot loop variables live here.
~4 ns. CPU's second-level cache. Larger (256 KB - 1 MB) but slower.
~100 ns. Random access to any byte in RAM. Redis operates entirely at this speed, which is why it's so fast.
~100 µs (100,000 ns). 1,000× slower than RAM. But SSDs can do ~100K IOPS randomly. For sequential reads, SSDs deliver ~500 MB/s to 3 GB/s (NVMe).
~10 ms (10,000,000 ns). 100× slower than SSD. Mechanical head must physically move. Sequential reads are ~100-200 MB/s. Avoid random reads on HDD at all costs.
~0.5 ms. This is why microservices in the same DC communicate fast. But 10 chained calls = 5ms — design for few hops.
~30-50 ms. Speed of light through fiber + router hops. This is why CDNs and regional replicas matter.
~100-200 ms. US to Europe ~100ms, US to Australia ~200ms. Users feel >100ms as 'sluggish'. This is why you need multi-region deployments for global apps.
~0.25 ms. Memory throughput is ~4-10 GB/s per channel.
~1 ms. NVMe SSDs can sustain ~3 GB/s sequential.
~20 ms. Only ~50-100 MB/s sequential on spinning disks.
~100K-200K ops/sec for simple GET/SET (single-threaded, in-memory, no disk I/O per operation). Pipeline mode can push to 1M ops/sec.
~5K-50K TPS depending on query complexity, indexing, and hardware. Simple key-value lookups on indexed columns: ~50K. Complex joins with sorting: ~1-5K.
~100K-500K messages/sec depending on message size. With small messages (~100 bytes), can exceed 1M msg/sec per broker.
Theoretically ~65K per IP (port range). Practically with connection pooling: 10K-100K concurrent connections. A WebSocket server can hold ~10K-50K persistent connections per instance.
86,400 — round to 100,000 (10^5) for quick math.
8.7 hours downtime per year. Three nines.
52.6 minutes downtime per year. Four nines — requires redundancy at every layer.
5.26 minutes downtime per year. Five nines — requires multi-region active-active with automated failover.

advanced_tweaks.technique: Use these numbers to challenge your own design
advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: After drawing HLD
advanced_tweaks.how: Ask yourself: 'My design does 3 sequential database reads per request, each ~5ms. That's 15ms just for DB. Add network hops, serialization, and application logic — I'm at ~50ms per request. I need 600K QPS. One server handles 600K/50ms = nope, that's 1000/(50ms) ≈ 20 QPS. I need 30,000 servers? That can't be right — I need caching!' This self-check catches design flaws before the interviewer does.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When designing request flow
advanced_tweaks.how: If your target is p99 < 200ms, allocate: network ingress/egress = 20ms, LB + API Gateway = 5ms, application logic = 25ms, cache lookup = 2ms, DB fallback (on cache miss) = 50ms, serialization = 5ms. Total = ~107ms with room to spare. If you have a cache hit rate of 95%, your average is even lower. This kind of reasoning impresses interviewers.

references.title: Jeff Dean's Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

children.title: Architecture Review Checklist & Decision Matrices
children.summary: A production-grade checklist to evaluate any system architecture and decision matrices for common technology choices.

explanation.overview: Before concluding your interview, double-check your architecture against these key criteria. In real life, this is the checklist Staff Engineers use during Architecture Review Board (ARB) meetings.

key_concepts.definition: If node X dies, does the system halt? Ensure every tier (LB, App, DB, Cache) has redundancy and automatic failover.
Where is the system constrained? CPU, Memory, Disk I/O, or Network Bandwidth? If user scale grows 10x, which box breaks first?
If a datacenter loses power right now, what data is permanently lost? Are writes acknowledged only after disk sync or while in memory?

examples.title: Decision Matrix: Database Selection

chapters.title: OOP & Low-Level Design Masterclass
chapters.summary: Master object-oriented programming, SOLID principles, GoF design patterns, and Domain-Driven Design (DDD) tactical patterns with real-world code examples and use cases.

explanation.overview: Low-Level Design (LLD) focuses on the internal structure of a single component — class hierarchies, design patterns, database schemas, and API contracts. While High-Level Design (HLD) asks 'what components do we need?', LLD asks 'how do we build each component?' LLD interviews test your ability to write clean, extensible, maintainable code that follows established industry principles.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: In an LLD interview (45-60 min), you are typically asked to design a specific component: a parking lot, an elevator system, a chess game, an LRU cache, or a rate limiter. You must produce class diagrams, identify entities, define relationships, apply relevant design patterns, and write working code. The evaluation focuses on extensibility (can new features be added without modifying existing code?), separation of concerns, and correct use of modern patterns.

children.title: OOP Core Concepts
children.summary: The four pillars of OOP and how they enable maintainable, extensible software.

explanation.overview: OOP organizes code around objects (data + behavior) rather than functions and procedures. Four pillars form its foundation.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Bundle data (fields) and methods into a single unit (class), and restrict direct access to internal state. External code interacts through public methods, preventing invalid state transitions. INDUSTRY TWEAK: Prefer immutable objects where possible (Java Records, Python dataclasses). Once created, state cannot change, eliminating entire categories of bugs like race conditions.

A class inherits fields and methods from a parent class, enabling 'is-a' relationships. DANGERS: Deep inheritance hierarchies (>3 levels) become fragile. INDUSTRY STANDARD: Prefer Composition over Inheritance ('has-a' instead of 'is-a'). It provides more flexibility to swap behaviors at runtime.

Objects of different classes can be treated through the same interface. Method overriding (runtime) enables plugin architectures. INTERNALLY: Runtime polymorphism works via dynamic dispatch (vtable lookup in the JVM).
Hide complex implementation details and expose only the essential interface. The caller doesn't know the underlying implementation. Interfaces and Abstract classes enforce this.

examples.title: Composition over Inheritance (TypeScript)
examples.description: Instead of a `Bird` class inheriting from `Animal` and a `RubberDuck` inheriting from `Bird` (which would awkwardly inherit a `fly()` method it shouldn't have), we compose behaviors.

examples.title: Real-World Architecture Decision Record (ADR): Composition vs Inheritance
examples.description: How a FAANG engineer documents an LLD design choice in an interview or design doc.
examples.code:
# ADR: Notification System Class Design

## Context
We are building a Notification Service that sends Email, SMS, and Push notifications. Some notifications are urgent, some are batched.

## Options Considered
1. Deep Inheritance: `UrgentEmailNotification extends EmailNotification extends BaseNotification`
2. Composition: `Notification(DeliveryStrategy, PriorityStrategy)`

## Decision
We chose **Composition**. 

## Consequences
* **Positive**: O(1) class scale. If we add 'Slack' and 'Delayed', we don't need a `DelayedSlackNotification` class. We just pass new strategies into the base `Notification` container.
* **Negative**: Slightly higher memory overhead due to multiple strategy object allocations per notification.

children.title: SOLID Principles — Deep Dive
children.summary: Five design principles that guide maintainable, extensible object-oriented code. Every LLD interviewer expects you to know these and apply them to your code.

explanation.overview: SOLID principles are guidelines that help you write code that is easy to change, test, and extend. They are the backbone of robust Low-Level Design.

key_concepts.definition: A class should have one and only one reason to change. If a class formats a report AND saves it to a database, it has two reasons to change. Split it.
Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to add new behavior without touching existing, tested code. Typically achieved using the Strategy Pattern.
Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness. A subclass should not throw unexpected exceptions or break base class invariants.
No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use. Create small, focused interfaces rather than large, 'fat' ones.
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Depend on interfaces, not concrete classes. This is the foundation of Dependency Injection.

examples.title: Applying OCP & DIP (Java)
examples.description: Refactoring an OrderService that violates Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion into a completely decoupled, extensible architecture.

children.title: Design Patterns — Essentials for Interviews
children.summary: The most frequently tested design patterns with internal mechanics, real-world constraints, and interview scenarios.

explanation.overview: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common software design problems. In interviews, applying the right pattern shows maturity. Do not force them; use them when the problem demands extensibility. In FAANG interviews, interviewers evaluate your language pragmatism. Java demands rigid interfaces and classes for patterns. Python's dynamic nature (functions as first-class citizens, duck typing) often renders explicit GoF patterns unnecessary or syntactically lighter.

key_concepts.definition: Ensures a class has exactly one instance globally. USE CASES: Database connection pools, configuration managers, thread pools.
Defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which instantiate. USE CASES: Cross-platform UI elements, picking different database drivers.
Construct complex objects step by step. Useful when a constructor has many optional parameters. USE CASES: Building complex SQL queries, generating API request payloads.

examples.title: Thread-Safe Singleton with Double-Checked Locking (Java)
examples.description: The industry standard way to write a lazy-loaded, thread-safe Singleton without taking a performance hit on every access.

examples.title: Singleton in Python (Metaclass approach)
examples.description: In Python, the most robust way to implement a Singleton is using a metaclass, ensuring any call to `Class()` returns the same instance.

examples.title: Factory Pattern (TypeScript / Spring Boot)
examples.description: A notification system where the factory determines which notification class to instantiate. In modern Java/Spring, this is often done using Dependency Injection rather than manual static factories.

use_cases.why: A Singleton ensures all parts of the application write logs to the exact same file stream to avoid write contention.

key_concepts.definition: Allows classes with incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping its own interface around that of an already existing class. USE CASES: Integrating third-party billing APIs with your legacy billing interface.

Provides a simplified interface to a larger, more complex body of code (a subsystem). USE CASES: Creating a simple `OrderProcessor.process()` that hides the complexity of `InventoryCheck`, `PaymentGateway`, and `ShippingService`.

Allows behavior to be added to an individual object, dynamically, without affecting the behavior of other objects from the same class. Solves the "subclass explosion" problem. USE CASES: Java `InputStream` wrappers, adding compression/encryption to streams.

examples.title: Adapter Pattern (Python)
examples.description: Adapting an old legacy XML billing system to work with a modern JSON interface.

use_cases.why: An API Gateway acts as a Facade. Mobile clients make a single call to `/api/dashboard`, and the gateway internally aggregates data from the UserService, PostService, and MentionService to return a single simplified JSON tree.

key_concepts.definition: Encapsulate a family of algorithms and make them interchangeable. The absolute most commonly tested pattern in LLD.
Define a one-to-many dependency. When one object (Subject) changes state, all dependents (Observers) are notified. The foundation of Event-Driven Architecture.

examples.title: Strategy Pattern: Parking Lot Pricing (Python / Spring)
examples.description: Strategy lets us swap pricing models at runtime. Python's functions-as-first-class-citizens means Strategy can often just be passing a function!

examples.title: Observer Pattern: Stock Ticker (TypeScript)
examples.description: A stock price updates, and multiple decoupled UI components need to react to the change.

use_cases.why: Use Strategy pattern to swap between Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window algorithms depending on the API endpoint configuration.
In-memory Pub/Sub systems in LLD interviews (like designing a local Kafka) rely entirely on the Observer pattern.

limitations: Language Over-engineering: Forcing Java-style strict object-oriented patterns into dynamic languages like Python or JavaScript often leads to unreadable "accidental complexity".

Pattern Blindness: Trying to fit a problem to a pattern rather than applying a pattern to solve a problem. If simple procedural code or functional composition solves it cleanly, don't force a Strategy pattern.
Singleton Testing Bottleneck: Singletons hold global state, which severely complicates unit testing because state bleeds across test cases.

children.title: Modern LLD: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Tactical Patterns
children.summary: Move beyond basic OOP to model complex business logic using Entities, Value Objects, and Aggregates.

explanation.overview: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) provides a structured approach to building complex software by aligning the code structure tightly with the business domain. Tactical DDD patterns are advanced LLD techniques that ensure data integrity and clean code boundaries.

key_concepts.definition: Objects that possess a distinct identity that persists over time, even if their attributes change. Example: A 'User' with ID 123 is the same user even if they change their email address. They encapsulate state and business logic.

Objects that have no conceptual identity; they are defined entirely by their attributes. They must be IMMUTABLE. Example: `Money(amount, currency)`, `Address(street, city, zip)`. If an address changes, you don't mutate the Address object; you replace it with a completely new Address object. WHY: Eliminates side-effects and makes code vastly easier to reason about.

A cluster of related Entities and Value Objects treated as a single unit for data changes. Every Aggregate has an 'Aggregate Root' (one specific Entity). RULE: External classes can ONLY hold references to the Aggregate Root, never to its internal children. The Root is responsible for enforcing all business invariants (rules) for the entire cluster.

examples.title: Entities vs Value Objects (Java)
examples.description: Showing how a mutable Order Entity is composed of immutable Money Value Objects.

use_cases.why: The Cart is the Aggregate Root. CartItems are internal entities. You cannot directly modify a CartItem from outside; you must call `cart.updateItemQuantity()`. This ensures the Cart can instantly recalculate its total and enforce rules like 'max 10 items per cart'.

children.title: LLD Interview Framework
children.summary: A structured 6-step approach to ace any low-level design interview.

step_by_step.title: Clarify Requirements & Constraints
step_by_step.detail: Ask: Who are the actors? What are the core use cases? Example for 'Design a Parking Lot': How many floors? Spot types (compact, large)? Payment required at exit gates?

step_by_step.title: Identify Core Entities & Enums
step_by_step.detail: List the nouns: ParkingLot, Floor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle (Car, Truck), Ticket. Define Enums: SpotType, VehicleType, TicketStatus.

step_by_step.title: Define APIs / Interfaces
step_by_step.detail: What operations exist? `parkVehicle(vehicle) -> Ticket`, `scanTicket(ticket) -> PaymentReceipt`. Define input/output.

step_by_step.title: Establish Relationships
step_by_step.detail: ParkingLot HAS-MANY Floors (composition). ParkingSpot HAS-A Vehicle (association). Draw a quick class diagram conceptually.

step_by_step.title: Apply Design Patterns
step_by_step.detail: Strategy pattern for Pricing. Factory for Ticket generation. Singleton for the ParkingLot instance.

step_by_step.title: Code with Concurrency edge cases
step_by_step.detail: Two cars arriving simultaneously trying to park in the last spot — use `ConcurrentHashMap` or a `ReadWriteLock` on spot assignment.

children.title: Advanced Machine Coding: Concurrency, State, & Edge Cases
children.summary: The secret to passing elite LLD/Machine Coding rounds: Designing thread-safe classes, handling concurrent access, and bulletproof error management.

explanation.overview: Senior developer blogs emphasize that elite machine coding rounds (like at Uber, Atlassian, or Flipkart) aren't just about drawing classes. They test your ability to write code that survives a multi-threaded, highly concurrent production environment where edge cases are the norm.

key_concepts.definition: If multiple threads call a method simultaneously, will the internal state corrupt? For example, in a Movie Ticket Booking system, two users clicking 'book' on the exact same seat simultaneously. FIX: Use thread-safe collections (`ConcurrentHashMap`), atomic variables (`AtomicInteger`), or explicit locking (`ReentrantLock`, `synchronized`). Prefer optimistic locking (CAS) for high read, low write scenarios, and pessimistic locking for high contention.

The easiest way to make a class thread-safe is to make it immutable. If internal state cannot change after instantiation, multiple threads can read it simultaneously without any locks. (e.g. representing a `Seat` as an immutable object, and keeping availability in a separate `AtomicBoolean`).

LLD code should never crash silently or throw generic `Exception`. Define custom domain exceptions (`SeatAlreadyBookedException`, `InsufficientFundsException`). Handle edge cases proactively: What happens if a user tries to split a $0 expense? What if a circular debt exists?

examples.title: Thread-Safe Booking System (Java)
examples.description: An example of handling concurrent bookings using ReentrantLock to ensure no double-booking occurs without locking the entire system.

use_cases.why: When stock runs low (e.g. only 1 copy of a book left), concurrent checkout requests must be serialized. Using a database transaction with `SELECT FOR UPDATE` simulates this at the DB level, but in an in-memory LLD round, you must use application-level locking.

children.title: LLD Evaluation Checklist & Decision Matrices
children.summary: A rubric-based checklist to self-evaluate your Low-Level Design before finishing the interview.

explanation.overview: Top candidates review their own designs before the interviewer points out flaws. Use this checklist to validate your LLD.

key_concepts.definition: If the interviewer asks 'Now add support for Crypto Payments', do you have to modify 5 existing classes, or just add 1 new class? If it's 5, you failed the Open/Closed Principle.
If two threads call your `bookTicket()` method at the exact same millisecond, what breaks? Have you identified the critical section and protected it with a Lock or Concurrent structure?

examples.title: Decision Matrix: Creational Patterns
examples.description: How to choose a creational pattern under interview pressure.
examples.code:
SCENARIO                          | PATTERN TO USE       | WHY
----------------------------------|----------------------|------------------------------------------
1 DB connection pool for the app  | Singleton            | Global access, costly to instantiate.
Choosing UI theme at runtime      | Factory Method       | Hides `if/else` instantiation logic.
Creating an HTTP Request          | Builder              | 10+ optional parameters, prevents giant constructor.
Copying a complex object          | Prototype            | Cheaper than creating from scratch via DB.

chapters.title: Key Characteristics of Distributed Systems
chapters.summary: The fundamental properties that define distributed systems — scalability, availability, reliability, consistency, and the trade-offs between them.

explanation.overview: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appear to users as a single coherent system. Every large-scale application (Google, Netflix, Amazon) is a distributed system. Understanding the key characteristics helps you make informed design decisions — every architecture is a set of trade-offs among these properties. DEVELOPER BLOG INSIGHT: 'Jumping from monolithic to distributed systems is like jumping from an acoustic guitar to a full symphony orchestra in a hurricane.'
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Distributed systems face challenges that monolithic systems don't: network is unreliable (packets drop, latency spikes), clocks are unsynchronized (each machine has slightly different time), nodes fail independently (one server crashes while others continue), and there's no shared memory (data must be explicitly communicated). These realities force you to make design trade-offs at every layer.

limitations: Network Unreliability: The Fallacies of Distributed Computing state the network is never 100% reliable. You must code for latency spikes, partitions, and dropped packets.
Increased Observability Overhead: When a request traverses 15 microservices, finding which one failed requires distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin) and centralized logging (ELK).
Data Consistency: Unlike a monolithic SQL database, enforcing ACID guarantees across multiple geographic regions is mathematically impossible without sacrificing availability (CAP Theorem).
common_mistakes: Assuming zero latency between internal microservices.
Failing to implement Circuit Breakers (like Resilience4j or PyBreaker) when talking to downstream dependencies.
Using distributed systems when a monolithic Postgres instance and a simple state API would suffice (YAGNI).

children.title: Scalability
children.summary: The ability of a system to handle increasing load by adding resources.

explanation.overview: Scalability is the system's capacity to cope with increased demand. A scalable system maintains performance (latency, throughput) as load grows — more users, more data, more requests.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Add more resources to a single machine — more CPU, RAM, SSD, faster network. EXAMPLE: upgrade from 16 GB RAM to 128 GB, or 4-core to 64-core CPU. PROS: simple (no code changes), no distributed system complexity, data consistency is easy (single machine). CONS: hardware limits (you can't buy a machine with 100 TB RAM), cost grows exponentially (a 64-core server costs more than 16× a 4-core), single point of failure (if this machine dies, everything dies). INDUSTRY USE: databases often scale vertically first — a beefier Postgres server can handle a lot more before you need sharding. Amazon RDS instances go up to 24 TB RAM and 128 vCPUs.

Add more machines to the pool. Each machine handles a portion of the load. EXAMPLE: instead of 1 server handling 10K QPS, use 10 servers each handling 1K QPS behind a load balancer. PROS: practically unlimited scale (just add more machines), fault tolerant (one machine fails, others continue), cost-effective (commodity hardware). CONS: code must be stateless (or state must be externalized to a shared store like Redis), distributed systems complexity (data partitioning, replication, consistency), network communication overhead. INDUSTRY STANDARD: application servers should ALWAYS be designed for horizontal scaling from day one. Store all state in databases/caches, make servers stateless, put a load balancer in front.

The ability to automatically add or remove resources based on current demand. Cloud auto-scaling: AWS Auto Scaling Groups monitor CPU/memory metrics and add/remove EC2 instances. Kubernetes HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) adjusts pod count based on CPU or custom metrics. CONFIGURABLE: min instances (floor — always running), max instances (ceiling — cost control), scaling metric (CPU > 70%, QPS > 1000, queue depth > 100), cooldown period (wait 300s after scaling before evaluating again, prevents oscillation). EDGE CASE: cold start — new instances take time to boot, load code, warm caches. During traffic spikes, there's a lag between the spike and the new capacity. FIX: keep a buffer of warm standby instances, or use provisioned capacity.

examples.title: Netflix Scaling Pattern
examples.description: Netflix serves 250M+ subscribers. Their microservices (100+) run on thousands of EC2 instances with auto-scaling. During peak hours (8-11 PM), auto-scaling adds instances. At 3 AM, it removes them. Databases use a mix: Aurora (relational, vertically scaled up to db.r5.24xlarge) for user accounts, Cassandra (horizontally scaled, 1000+ nodes) for viewing history/recommendations.

examples.title: Failure Modes & Exception Handling
examples.description: How to handle catastrophic failures and network partitions in this tier.
examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

configurable_params.name: Library Configuration Parameters
configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Tuning configuration to drop stale packets reduces latency but requires robust frontend exception handling.

children.title: Availability
children.summary: The percentage of time a system is operational and accessible.

explanation.overview: Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime). It's usually expressed as 'nines': 99% (two nines) = 3.65 days downtime/year. 99.9% (three nines) = 8.76 hours. 99.99% (four nines) = 52.6 minutes. 99.999% (five nines) = 5.26 minutes.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Achieving high availability requires eliminating single points of failure (SPOF) at every layer. For each component, ask: 'if this dies, does the system stop working?' If yes, add redundancy. Load Balancer SPOF: deploy 2 LBs with floating IP (VIP) and keepalived/VRRP failover. App Server SPOF: run N instances behind LB; N-1 can handle full load. Database SPOF: primary + synchronous standby replica with automatic failover (Patroni for Postgres, RDS Multi-AZ). Cache SPOF: Redis Sentinel or Cluster mode for auto-failover. DNS SPOF: use multiple DNS providers (Cloudflare + Route 53).

key_concepts.definition: SLI (Service Level Indicator): the actual measurement (e.g., request success rate = 99.95% this month). SLO (Service Level Objective): the target (e.g., 'availability must be ≥ 99.9%'). SLA (Service Level Agreement): the contract with customers (e.g., 'if availability drops below 99.9%, customer gets service credits'). Google's SRE book: alert when burning through your error budget too fast, not on individual incidents.

Components in series (sequential dependency): overall = A1 × A2 × A3. If each is 99.9%, overall = 99.7%. Components in parallel (redundant): overall = 1 - (1-A1)(1-A2). Two 99.9% components in parallel = 1 - 0.001² = 99.9999%. IMPLICATION: minimize sequential dependencies (reduce the critical path). Add redundancy (parallel components) for each critical component.

Active-Passive (warm standby): primary handles traffic, standby replicates data. On primary failure, standby takes over (seconds to minutes). Active-Active: both nodes serve traffic simultaneously. On failure of one, the other absorbs its load. More complex (must handle conflicts) but zero-downtime failover. Multi-Region Active-Active: deploy in 2+ AWS regions. Route 53 health checks route traffic away from unhealthy regions automatically. This is how AWS, Google, and Netflix achieve five nines.

examples.title: AWS DynamoDB Outage Case Study (Cascading Failure)
examples.description: A textbook example of how a failure in a foundational service (DNS/Metadata) can cascade and take down a global distributed database.
examples.code:
What Happened:
An underlying sub-system responsible for metadata and DNS management experienced a latent race condition. When a network partition occurred, nodes began heavily querying the DNS management system to re-establish topology.

The Cascade:
The overwhelming query volume overwhelmed the metadata service, causing it to drop requests. Because nodes couldn't get metadata, they assumed more nodes had failed, sending EVEN MORE metadata requests. This recursive retry loop acts as a self-inflicted Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Always discuss 'Thundering Herds' and Cascading Failures. The fix is to implement strict Circuit Breakers and Exponential Backoff + Jitter on all internal inter-service retries.

children.title: Reliability & Fault Tolerance
children.summary: The ability of a system to continue functioning correctly even when components fail.

explanation.overview: Reliability means the system performs its intended function correctly under stated conditions for a specified period. Fault tolerance is a subset — continuing to operate (possibly at degraded capacity) when components fail. The key insight: failures are inevitable at scale. With 10,000 servers, several fail every day. A reliable system is designed EXPECTING failure.

key_concepts.definition: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): average time between system failures. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair): average time to restore service after failure. Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). To improve availability, either increase MTBF (better hardware, redundancy) or decrease MTTR (automation, runbooks, observability). Netflix philosophy: focus on reducing MTTR rather than preventing all failures.

Active redundancy: multiple components active simultaneously (RAID-1 disk mirroring, load-balanced servers). Passive redundancy: standby component activated on failure (hot standby database). No redundancy: if it fails, feature is unavailable (acceptable for non-critical features like 'Related Products' on Amazon — main purchase flow still works).

Intentionally inject failures in production to verify the system recovers correctly. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production EC2 instances. Chaos Kong simulates entire region outage. Latency Monkey injects network delays. WHY: proves your failover actually works, not just in theory but in practice. Finds weaknesses before real outages expose them. IMPLEMENTATION: start in staging, gradually move to production. Define 'steady state' (normal metrics), hypothesize what happens during failure, run experiment, observe if system recovers within SLO.

When a component fails, the system continues with reduced functionality rather than total failure. EXAMPLE: if the recommendation engine is down, Amazon still shows the product page — just without 'Customers also bought'. If the cache is down, the system falls back to database (slower but functional). If a non-critical microservice is down, the API returns partial data with a flag indicating degraded mode. IMPLEMENTATION: circuit breakers (see ch13), fallback methods, feature flags to disable failing features.

examples.title: Circuit Breakers in Java & Python
examples.description: To prevent cascading failures, top engineering blogs recommend the Circuit Breaker pattern. It stops requests to a failing service immediately, giving it time to recover rather than overwhelming it.

children.title: Consistency Models
children.summary: Different levels of data consistency guarantees and when to use each in distributed systems.

explanation.overview: When data is replicated across multiple nodes, reads from different nodes may return different values. Consistency models define what guarantees the system provides about what value a read returns.

key_concepts.definition: Every read returns the most recent write, as if there's only one copy of the data. After a write completes, all subsequent reads (from any node) see the new value. HOW: all writes go through a single leader (or consensus protocol like Raft), and reads also go to the leader (or use quorum reads). COST: higher latency (must wait for consensus), lower availability (during partition, CP systems refuse requests). WHEN: financial transactions (bank balance must be accurate), inventory management (must not oversell), user authentication (password change must take effect immediately).

If no new writes occur, eventually all replicas converge to the same value. Reads may return stale data for a window of time (typically milliseconds to seconds). HOW: writes go to any node (or leader), and replicate asynchronously. Reads can go to any node. COST: you may read stale data. BENEFIT: lower latency (no waiting for replication), higher availability (works during partitions). WHEN: social media feeds (seeing a tweet 3 seconds late is fine), DNS (TTL-based propagation), CDN cache (eventually consistent with origin). IMPLEMENTATION: Dynamo-style databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB) with tunable consistency — write to W nodes, read from R nodes. If W + R > N, you get strong consistency. If not, eventual.

If operation A causally precedes operation B (B depends on A's result), then every node sees A before B. Unrelated operations can be seen in any order. EXAMPLE: User posts a photo (A), then comments on it (B). B causally depends on A. Every reader must see the photo before the comment. But another user's unrelated post (C) can appear in any order relative to A and B. HOW: use vector clocks or Lamport timestamps to track causal ordering. Each message carries a logical clock that recipients use to order operations. COST: more complex than eventual, less expensive than strong. Used by: MongoDB (causal consistency sessions).

A user always sees their own writes. After you update your profile picture, you must see the new picture on refresh (even if other users temporarily see the old one). IMPLEMENTATION: route the user's reads to the same replica they wrote to (using sticky sessions or a 'recent write' flag that routes to the leader for a short window after writes).

Once a user sees a value at time T, they never see an older value on subsequent reads. Without this, a user might see their feed at 10:00 AM, refresh and see it at 9:55 AM (reading from a lagging replica), then refresh again and see 10:00 AM. IMPLEMENTATION: pin the user to a specific replica (sticky sessions) or track the user's last-seen timestamp and only serve from replicas at least as fresh.

examples.title: Implementing Tunable Consistency (Quorum Read) in Python
examples.description: How a masterless distributed database (like Cassandra) resolves conflicts during a Read operation when W + R > N.
examples.code:
import asyncio

# Simulating network calls to 3 replicas (N=3)
async def fetch_from_replica(replica_id, key):
    # Returns (value, vector_clock_timestamp)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    # Simulating divergent state: replica 3 has stale data
    if replica_id == 3:
        return {"value": "old_state", "ts": 100}
    return {"value": "new_state", "ts": 105}

async def quorum_read(key, R=2):
    # Fire requests to all 3 replicas, but we only wait for R (2) responses
    tasks = [fetch_from_replica(i, key) for i in range(1, 4)]
    
    # asyncio.as_completed yields results as they arrive
    responses = []
    for coro in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):
        result = await coro
        responses.append(result)
        if len(responses) == R:
            break # Short-circuit once we satisfy the Read Quorum!
            
    # Conflict Resolution: Return the response with the highest timestamp (LWW)
    best_response = max(responses, key=lambda x: x['ts'])
    print(f"Read Quorum satisfied. Winning value: {best_response['value']}")
    return best_response['value']

asyncio.run(quorum_read('user:123', R=2))

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When you need tunable consistency. Read/Write nodes (R/W) must overlap: W + R > N (Total Replicas).
advanced_tweaks.how: If N=3, W=2, R=2 ensures strong consistency because every Read checks at least 2 nodes, guaranteeing it sees the latest write (which hit at least 2 nodes).

chapters.title: Networking & Communication Protocols
chapters.summary: Complete networking guide — OSI/TCP-IP layers, DNS resolution, TCP vs UDP internals, HTTP evolution, REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL, WebSockets, and protocol selection for system design.

explanation.overview: Every system design involves components communicating over a network. Understanding protocols — their strengths, weaknesses, and internals — lets you make informed choices about how services talk to each other. This chapter covers everything from low-level TCP to high-level API paradigms. DEVELOPER BLOG INSIGHT: 'There is no perfect protocol; every choice is a trade-off between latency, throughput, complexity, and payload size.'
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Network communication follows a layered model. Each layer adds its own header and handles a specific concern: physical transmission (L1-L2), addressing and routing (L3 IP), reliable delivery (L4 TCP/UDP), and application semantics (L7 HTTP/gRPC). When you type a URL, your request traverses all these layers down on the client, crosses the network, and traverses up on the server.

limitations: gRPC Debugging: Because Protobuf is binary, you cannot just use `curl` or browser dev tools easily to inspect payloads. You need specific tooling like `grpcurl` or BloomRPC.

WebSocket Scaling: Unlike stateless REST requests, WebSockets hold an open file descriptor on the server. To scale 1M concurrent users, you need dedicated connection handling servers and a Pub/Sub backplane (like Redis or Kafka) to route messages across instances.
HTTP/3 (QUIC) Adoption: While excellent for mobile networks (handles packet loss better than TCP), many enterprise firewalls heavily throttle or block UDP traffic, forcing fallbacks to HTTP/2.
common_mistakes: Choosing gRPC for a public-facing API without realizing browsers need a translation proxy (gRPC-Web).
Overusing WebSockets for simple request-response flows where long-polling or Server-Sent Events (SSE) would be drastically simpler.
Ignoring TLS handshake overhead in low-latency internal microservices (often internal microservices use plain HTTP/2 or mutual TLS depending on zero-trust policies).

children.title: DNS — Domain Name System
children.summary: How domain names are resolved to IP addresses — the hierarchical resolution process, record types, and DNS-based tricks for system design.

explanation.overview: DNS is the internet's phone book — it translates human-readable domain names (google.com) to IP addresses (142.250.80.46). Every HTTP request begins with a DNS lookup.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: RESOLUTION CHAIN (iterative): (1) Browser checks its local DNS cache. (2) If miss, OS resolver checks /etc/hosts then OS DNS cache. (3) If miss, query the configured DNS resolver (ISP or public like 8.8.8.8). (4) Resolver queries Root nameserver (13 clusters worldwide, anycast) → gets referral to .com TLD nameserver. (5) Resolver queries .com TLD nameserver → gets referral to google.com's authoritative nameserver (ns1.google.com). (6) Resolver queries authoritative nameserver → gets the A record (IP address). (7) Resolver caches the result (respects TTL) and returns to client. Total time: 50-200ms for uncached lookup, <1ms for cached. RECORD TYPES: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another domain), MX (mail server), NS (nameserver), TXT (text — used for SPF, DKIM, domain verification), SRV (service discovery — host + port). TTL (Time To Live): how long resolvers cache the record. Low TTL (60s) = fast failover but more DNS queries. High TTL (86400s = 1 day) = fewer queries but slow failover.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: DNS-based load balancing: return multiple A records (round-robin). Route 53 weighted routing: 70% traffic to region A, 30% to region B. Latency-based routing: resolve to the closest datacenter. Health checks: automatically remove unhealthy IPs from DNS responses. GeoDNS: resolve to different IPs based on client's geographic location (Cloudflare, Route 53). EDGE CASE: DNS caching means changes take time to propagate. During a migration, set TTL to 60s days before, then switch IPs, then raise TTL back. Some clients ignore TTL (especially Java's default DNS cache timeout of infinity — override with networkaddress.cache.ttl=30).

Multiple servers share the same IP address. BGP routing sends each client to the nearest server. Used by CDNs (Cloudflare has 300+ PoPs, all sharing the same anycast IP) and DNS root servers (13 addresses but hundreds of physical servers).

examples.title: Facebook 2021 Global Outage Case Study (BGP & DNS)
examples.description: A catastrophic failure demonstrating what happens when DNS and BGP routing fail simultaneously at a global scale.
examples.code:
What Happened:
During a routine maintenance job, Facebook engineers issued a command to assess global backbone capacity. A bug in the audit tool caused it to inadvertently take down all connections in the backbone network.

The Cascade:
Because the backbone went down, Facebook's DNS servers (which announce their IP addresses via BGP - Border Gateway Protocol) suddenly stopped announcing their routes to the global internet. To the rest of the world, Facebook's IP addresses effectively ceased to exist.

The Catch-22:
Engineers could not fix the issue remotely because the internal secure management network relied on the very DNS that was down. They had to physically travel to data centers, log into physical routers, and manually override the configurations.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Always separate the Control Plane (management tools) from the Data Plane (user traffic). If your management tools rely on the same network they manage, a failure locks you out.
