chapters.title: Concurrency & Synchronization
chapters.summary: Concurrency primitives (mutex, semaphore, spinlock, RW-lock), Java memory model, concurrency patterns (producer-consumer, reactor), deadlock detection, and distributed transactions.

explanation.overview: Concurrency is about multiple operations executing in overlapping time periods. Parallelism is about executing simultaneously on multiple cores. In system design, concurrency appears at every level: multiple threads handling requests, multiple servers processing jobs, multiple database clients competing for rows. Understanding concurrency primitives lets you reason about race conditions, deadlocks, and correctness.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: At the CPU level, a single core can only execute one instruction at a time. The OS scheduler rapidly switches between threads (context switch ~1-10µs), creating the illusion of simultaneous execution. On multi-core CPUs, true parallelism occurs. The challenge: when multiple threads access shared mutable state without synchronization, you get race conditions — the result depends on unpredictable timing.

key_concepts.definition: Binary lock: owned by one thread at a time. Other threads calling lock() are put to sleep (blocked) by the OS until the owner calls unlock(). INTERNAL: on Linux, mutex uses futex (fast userspace mutex). The fast path (no contention) is a single atomic CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instruction in userspace — no kernel involvement (~25ns). Only on contention does it syscall into the kernel to sleep the thread. Reentrant mutex: the same thread can acquire it multiple times (maintains a count, must release same number of times). USE: protecting shared data structures (hash maps, queues, counters).

Counter-based synchronization. Initialized with count N. acquire() decrements count. If count < 0, thread blocks. release() increments count. If a thread is waiting, wake it. Binary semaphore (N=1) ≈ mutex but not owned by any thread (any thread can release). Counting semaphore (N>1): limit concurrent access. EXAMPLE: connection pool of 10 connections — semaphore(10). Each thread acquires before using a connection, releases after.

Loop (spin) checking a flag via atomic CAS until it succeeds. Does NOT put the thread to sleep — wastes CPU cycles while waiting. WHEN TO USE: only when the critical section is very short (< 1µs) and context switch cost (1-10µs) exceeds expected wait time. Linux kernel uses spinlocks for short sections where sleeping is not allowed (interrupt handlers). NEVER use in application code for long waits.

Atomic CPU instruction: CAS(addr, expected, new) — if *addr == expected, set *addr = new and return true. Otherwise return false. Foundation of all lock-free data structures. Java AtomicInteger.compareAndSet(), C++ std::atomic. LOCK-FREE COUNTER: instead of mutex { counter++ }, do: loop { old = counter; if CAS(counter, old, old+1) break; }. No blocking, no sleeping — if another thread modified counter between read and CAS, CAS fails and we retry. ABA problem: value changes A→B→A and CAS can't detect it. FIX: use versioned CAS (AtomicStampedReference in Java).

Allows multiple concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. Readers don't block other readers (shared mode), but a writer blocks all readers and writers (exclusive mode). USE: read-heavy data structures (config, caches read 100× more than written). INTERNAL: maintains reader_count + writer flag. reader.lock(): if no writer, increment reader_count. writer.lock(): wait for reader_count=0 and no other writer. STARVATION: writers can starve if readers keep arriving. FIX: fair RW lock (writers get priority after waiting).

examples.title: Java HashMap Infinite Loop Race Condition
examples.description: A famous, recurring production outage caused by using a non-thread-safe data structure in a concurrent environment.
examples.code:
The Bug:
Prior to Java 8, the standard `java.util.HashMap` used a linked list for collision resolution. When the map reached its capacity, it triggered a `resize()` operation to double the array size and rehash all elements.

The Race Condition:
If two threads triggered `resize()` simultaneously without external synchronization, race conditions during the transfer of nodes from the old array to the new array could corrupt the linked list pointers. specifically, it could create a circular reference (Node A -> Node B -> Node A).

The Cascade:
The next time any thread attempted to `get()` an element that hashed to that bucket, it would enter an infinite while loop traversing the circular linked list. The thread's CPU usage instantly spiked to 100%. As more requests hit that bucket, more threads got trapped in the infinite loop. Within minutes, the entire server cluster would experience 100% CPU exhaustion and total unresponsiveness.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Never share mutable, non-thread-safe data structures across threads. Always use explicitly concurrent structures like `ConcurrentHashMap` which use lock striping and CAS operations to allow safe, highly concurrent reads and writes.

PRIMITIVE          | PERFORMANCE COST | BLOCKING? | BEST USED FOR

Mutex (Lock)       | Medium (Syscall) | Yes       | General purpose sharing (protecting block of code)
Read-Write Lock    | Medium           | Yes       | Data structures read 100x more frequently than written
Atomic (CAS)       | Very Low         | No        | Simple counters, lock-free queues, tight loops
Semaphore          | Medium           | Yes       | Limiting concurrent access to finite resource pool (DB conns)
Spinlock           | Variable (CPU)   | No        | Microsecond-level critical sections inside OS kernels

key_concepts.definition: Producers put items into a bounded buffer (BlockingQueue). Consumers take items from the buffer. Buffer decouples production rate from consumption rate. INTERNAL: BlockingQueue uses a mutex + two condition variables (not_empty, not_full). put(): lock → if full, wait(not_full) → insert → signal(not_empty) → unlock. take(): lock → if empty, wait(not_empty) → remove → signal(not_full) → unlock. Java: ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue. USE: request processing (web server puts requests in queue, worker threads consume), Kafka consumer pattern.

Pre-create a fixed number of threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue; idle threads pick up tasks. Prevents thread explosion (creating a new thread per request = 10K threads = excessive context switching + OOM). Java: ExecutorService with ThreadPoolExecutor(coreSize, maxSize, keepAlive, queue). CONFIGURABLE: corePoolSize (always running), maximumPoolSize (upper limit), queueCapacity (buffer), rejectionPolicy (AbortPolicy throws exception, CallerRunsPolicy runs on submitter's thread). SIZING: CPU-bound tasks: threads = num_cores. I/O-bound tasks: threads = num_cores × (1 + wait_time/compute_time). If compute=5ms, wait=50ms: threads = 8 × (1+10) = 88.

Single thread runs an event loop that multiplexes I/O across many connections. Used by: Node.js, Redis, NGINX, Netty. HOW: one thread calls epoll_wait() → gets list of ready sockets → processes each → loops. Non-blocking I/O: if an operation would block (disk read, network write), register a callback and continue processing other events. The callback is invoked when the operation completes. ADVANTAGE: handles thousands of concurrent connections with one thread (no context switching overhead). DISADVANTAGE: CPU-bound work blocks the entire event loop. FIX: offload CPU-heavy work to worker threads or a thread pool.

Two or more threads are waiting for each other to release locks, creating a cycle. Four necessary conditions (Coffman): (1) Mutual Exclusion: resource held exclusively. (2) Hold and Wait: thread holds one lock while waiting for another. (3) No Preemption: locks can't be forcibly taken. (4) Circular Wait: thread A waits for B, B waits for A. PREVENTION: break any one condition. Lock ordering: always acquire locks in a fixed global order (by lock ID). Breaks circular wait. Timeout: tryLock(timeout) — give up after N ms. Breaks hold-and-wait. DETECTION: build a wait-for graph (nodes = threads, edge = A waits for B's lock). If the graph has a cycle, deadlock exists. Kill one thread in the cycle (victim selection).

chapters.title: Rate Limiting
chapters.summary: Rate limiting algorithms with internals — Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed/Sliding Window — distributed rate limiting, and response headers.

explanation.overview: Rate limiting controls the number of requests a client can make in a time window. It protects your system from abuse (DDoS), ensures fair usage among clients, prevents resource exhaustion, and enforces billing tiers. Every production API has rate limiting — typically implemented at the API Gateway or Load Balancer layer.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: A bucket holds up to C tokens (capacity). Tokens are added at rate R per second. Each request consumes 1 token. If bucket is empty, request is rejected (429 Too Many Requests). IMPLEMENTATION: don't run a timer to add tokens. Instead, compute tokens lazily: on each request, calculate tokens_available = min(C, stored_tokens + R × (now - last_refill_time)). If tokens_available >= 1, allow and decrement. Store: {tokens: float, last_refill: timestamp}. In Redis: two keys per client (tokens + last_refill), updated atomically with a Lua script. BEHAVIOR: allows bursts up to C tokens, then sustains at rate R. Example: C=10, R=2/sec. A client can burst 10 requests instantly, then 2/sec thereafter. CONFIGURABLE: C controls burst size. R controls sustained rate. Different buckets for different endpoints (/api = 100/min, /search = 20/min). USED BY: AWS API Gateway, Stripe, GitHub API.

INTERNAL: requests enter a queue (bucket). The queue drains at a fixed rate R. If the queue is full (capacity C), new requests are dropped. Unlike token bucket, leaky bucket smooths output — no bursts. Output rate is always exactly R, regardless of how bursty the input is. IMPLEMENTATION: use a FIFO queue. A scheduler dequeues and processes at rate R. If queue.size >= C, reject. USE WHEN: you need a perfectly smooth request rate (bandwidth shaping, network traffic policing).

INTERNAL: divide time into fixed windows (60-second intervals). Each window has a counter starting at 0. Each request increments the counter. If counter > limit, reject. At window boundary, counter resets. IMPLEMENTATION (Redis): key = rate_limit:{client_id}:{window_start}. INCR key, EXPIRE key 60. Very simple, O(1) per request. PROBLEM: boundary burst — a client can send limit requests at 00:59 and limit requests at 01:00, effectively getting 2× limit in a 1-second window. FIX: sliding window.

INTERNAL: store the timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis ZADD). On each request: remove entries older than window_size ago (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), count remaining entries (ZCARD), if count < limit, add current timestamp (ZADD). ACCURATE: no boundary issues. EXPENSIVE: stores one entry per request. 1000 requests/minute × 1M users = 1B entries. Too much memory. USE: when accuracy matters and traffic is low.

INTERNAL: combines fixed window with weighted averaging. Keep counters for current window and previous window. Estimated count = prev_window_count × overlap_percentage + curr_window_count. Example: 60-second windows. We're 15 seconds into the current window. Previous window had 45 requests. Current window has 18 requests. Estimated rate = 45 × (45/60) + 18 = 45 × 0.75 + 18 = 33.75 + 18 = 51.75. If limit is 60, allow. IMPLEMENTATION: just two counters (2 Redis keys per client). O(1) memory. Error < 0.003% in practice. USED BY: Cloudflare for their rate limiting. This is the industry-standard algorithm — simple, memory-efficient, and accurate enough.

examples.title: Stripe's 4-Dimensional Rate Limiting Architecture
examples.description: How Stripe, a developer-first financial API, uses multiple concurrent rate limiters to guarantee platform stability without punishing legitimate users.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Stripe processes billions of API calls for payments globally. A simple '100 requests per second' limit per user is insufficient because some operations (like creating a charge) are highly resource-intensive, while others (like retrieving a past transaction) are cheap.

The Architecture (4 Types of Limiters):
Stripe employs four distinct types of rate limiters simultaneously:
1. Request Rate Limiters: The standard API limit (e.g., 100 req/sec per user). Uses a fast Redis Token Bucket.
2. Concurrent Requests Limiters: Prevents resource exhaustion from slow endpoints. If a user tries to run 50 simultaneous heavy 'Search' queries that each take 2 seconds, they are blocked even if their req/sec limit is high.
3. Fleet Usage Limiters: Limits total platform traffic across all users. If Stripe's internal capacity is dwindling during Black Friday, they throttle lower-priority API calls globally to ensure critical payments always process.
4. Worker Utilization Limiters: If a specific backend service (e.g., the Webhook Sender) is overloaded, it sheds load by returning 429s specifically for that service, preserving the rest of the API.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Advanced rate limiting is not just about counting HTTP requests. It's about protecting backend compute, managing concurrency, and prioritizing critical business paths over non-critical ones.

key_concepts.definition: All rate limit state in Redis. Every request checks Redis via Lua script (atomic INCR + EXPIRE). PROS: accurate (single source of truth, no over-allowance). CONS: Redis is a SPOF for rate limiting (if Redis is down, do you allow all or deny all?). Added latency (~0.5ms per request). FIX for SPOF: fail open (allow all requests if Redis is down) for most APIs. Fail closed (block all) for critical endpoints (payment, login).

Each app server maintains local rate limit counters. Periodically sync with central store (every 1-5 seconds). Between syncs, each server allows limit/num_servers requests. PROS: no single point of failure, no per-request latency to Redis. CONS: allows slight over-limit (up to num_servers × overage_per_server). Acceptable for most use cases — rate limits are soft boundaries.

Always return rate limit info in response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 (max requests per window), X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42 (requests left in current window), X-RateLimit-Reset: 1710456789 (Unix timestamp when window resets), Retry-After: 30 (seconds to wait, included with 429 response).

examples.title: Token Bucket Implementation via Redis Lua Scripting
examples.description: A production-grade algorithmic snippet ensuring perfectly atomic distributed rate limiting without CPU loops or race conditions.
examples.code:
-- The Redis KEYs and ARGs provided by the application
local tokens_key = KEYS[1]
local timestamp_key = KEYS[2]

local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4])

-- Fetch current state limit per client
local last_tokens = tonumber(redis.call("get", tokens_key))
if last_tokens == nil then
    last_tokens = capacity
end

local last_refreshed = tonumber(redis.call("get", timestamp_key))
if last_refreshed == nil then
    last_refreshed = 0
end

local delta = math.max(0, now - last_refreshed)
-- Refill based on time elapsed
local filled_tokens = math.min(capacity, last_tokens + (delta * rate))
local allowed = filled_tokens >= requested
local new_tokens = filled_tokens

if allowed then
    -- Consume tokens
    new_tokens = filled_tokens - requested
end

-- Update Redis keys unconditionally
redis.call("setex", tokens_key, 60, new_tokens)
redis.call("setex", timestamp_key, 60, now)

return { allowed, new_tokens }

chapters.title: Resiliency, Security & Architecture Patterns
chapters.summary: Resiliency patterns (circuit breaker 3-state machine, retry with jitter, bulkhead), security internals (TLS 1.3, JWT, OAuth 2.0), and cloud architecture patterns.

explanation.overview: Real production systems fail constantly. Resilient systems don't prevent all failures — they isolate them, recover quickly, and degrade gracefully. Security ensures that only authorized users can access data and that data is protected in transit and at rest. Architecture patterns provide reusable solutions for common system evolution challenges.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: CLOSED (normal): requests pass through. Track failure count. When failures reach threshold (e.g., 5 failures in 60 seconds), transition to OPEN. OPEN: all requests fail immediately (fast-fail) without calling the downstream service. After a timeout period (e.g., 30 seconds), transition to HALF-OPEN. HALF-OPEN: allow ONE probe request through. If it succeeds, transition back to CLOSED (service recovered). If it fails, transition back to OPEN (still down). INTERNAL STATE: {state: CLOSED|OPEN|HALF_OPEN, failure_count: int, last_failure_time: timestamp, success_count_in_half_open: int}. CONFIGURABLE: failure_threshold (5), timeout_duration (30s), success_threshold_in_half_open (3). WHY: prevents cascading failures. If Service B is down, Service A's circuit breaker fast-fails instead of timing out on every request (saving thread pool resources and response time). TOOLS: Resilience4j (Java), Polly (.NET), Hystrix (deprecated Netflix), Envoy (built-in circuit breaking).

On transient failure (network timeout, 503), retry after increasing delays. Formula: wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt) + random_jitter. Example: base=100ms, cap=30s. Attempt 1: 100ms + jitter. Attempt 2: 200ms + jitter. Attempt 3: 400ms + jitter. ... Attempt 8: 25.6s + jitter. WHY JITTER: without jitter, all clients that failed at the same time retry at the same time (thundering herd retry storm). Jitter spreads retries randomly. Types: Full jitter: wait = random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)). Equal jitter: wait = min(cap, base × 2^attempt)/2 + random(0, min(cap, base × 2^attempt)/2). ONLY retry on transient errors (timeout, 503, 429). NEVER retry on permanent errors (400, 404, 403).

Isolate resources so failure in one area doesn't affect others. Named after ship bulkhead compartments. IMPLEMENTATION: separate thread pools per downstream service. Service A gets thread pool of 20. Service B gets thread pool of 20. If Service A is slow and all 20 threads are blocked, Service B's pool is unaffected — it continues serving normally. Without bulkhead: a slow downstream blocks all shared threads, and the entire server becomes unresponsive. Envoy proxy: configurable max_connections and max_pending_requests per upstream cluster.

ALWAYS set timeouts on every external call. Without timeouts, a hung downstream service blocks your threads indefinitely. DEADLINE PROPAGATION: pass the remaining time budget downstream. If the client set a 5-second deadline and your service spent 2 seconds so far, pass 3 seconds to the downstream call. If the downstream can't complete in 3 seconds, it fast-fails. gRPC has built-in deadline propagation. For REST: pass deadline as a header (X-Request-Deadline: unix_timestamp).

examples.title: Netflix Chaos Engineering & Hystrix Fallbacks
examples.description: How Netflix built the Simian Army to intentionally break production systems, forcing developers to build resilient software.
examples.code:
The Problem:
When Netflix migrated to AWS, they realized that in a massive distributed environment, EC2 instances drop, networks partition, and downstream dependencies periodically fail. Assuming 99.9% availability per microservice, a call chain of 100 microservices yields only 90.4% total uptime.

The Architecture (Hystrix & Chaos Monkey):
1. The Hystrix Circuit Breaker: Netflix built 'Hystrix' to wrap every external call in a circuit breaker with a strict timeout and an isolated thread pool (Bulkhead pattern). If a downstream recommendation service hung, Hystrix would instantly fast-fail the request rather than exhausting Netflix's Tomcat connection pool.
2. Graceful Fallbacks: When Hystrix tripped, it didn't just throw an error. It triggered a fallback function. If the 'personalized recommendations' service failed, Hystrix returned an old cached list, or a hardcoded list of 'Top 10 Globally' movies. The user never saw an error.
3. Chaos Monkey: To guarantee these fallbacks actually worked, Netflix created Chaos Monkey, a script that randomly terminated production EC2 instances during business hours. This forced engineers to design stateless, resilient microservices where the loss of any single node was invisible to the user.

Takeaway for Interviews:
True resiliency isn't about preventing servers from going down; it's about anticipating failure. Always design 'degraded modes.' If the search system fails, can you offer a basic category browse? If the database fails, can you serve a stale cache?

examples.title: Circuit Breaker Implementation in Python
examples.description: A bare-bones implementation of the 3-state Circuit Breaker state machine (Closed, Open, Half-Open).
examples.code:
import time
import random
from enum import Enum

class State(Enum):
    CLOSED = 1
    OPEN = 2
    HALF_OPEN = 3

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=5):
        self.state = State.CLOSED
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.last_failure_time = None

    def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == State.OPEN:
            if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.recovery_timeout:
                print("Timeout elapsed. State -> HALF_OPEN. Allowing 1 test request.")
                self.state = State.HALF_OPEN
            else:
                raise Exception("Circuit is OPEN. Fast-failing request.")

        try:
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                print("Half-Open test succeeded! State -> CLOSED. Resetting counters.")
                self.state = State.CLOSED
                self.failures = 0
            return result
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.failures += 1
            self.last_failure_time = time.time()
            print(f"Call failed. Failure {self.failures}/{self.failure_threshold}.")
            
            if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                print("Threshold reached! State -> OPEN.")
                self.state = State.OPEN
            raise e

# Usage:
# cb = CircuitBreaker()
# try:
#     result = cb.call(fetch_data_from_flakey_payment_api, payload)
# except Exception:
#     result = get_cached_fallback_data()

examples.title: Resiliency Pattern Decision Matrix
examples.description: Which fault-tolerance pattern to apply in an interview based on the failure behavior of the downstream dependency.
examples.code:
FAILURE SCENARIO             | CORRECT PATTERN           | DESCRIPTION
-----------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------
Transient Network Glitch     | Retry with Jitter/Backoff | Retry immediately, then wait longer. Add jitter to prevent storm.
Downstream DB is Dead        | Circuit Breaker           | Stop calling it. Fast-fail immediately. Periodically test (Half-Open).
Slow / Hung Downstream       | Timeouts + Bulkheads      | Strict deadlines. Isolate thread pools so a slow service doesn't drain caller.
Sudden Traffic Spike         | Rate Limiting / Load Shed | Drop requests shedding bottom-tier traffic to save core infrastructure.
Unavailable Crucial Service  | Graceful Fallback         | Serve stale cache, default data, or simplified UI instead of 500 Error.

key_concepts.definition: Stateless authentication token: Header.Payload.Signature (base64-encoded). Header: {alg: 'RS256', typ: 'JWT'}. Payload: {user_id: 123, role: 'admin', exp: 1710456789}. Signature: HMAC-SHA256(header + '.' + payload, secret_key) or RSA signature for asymmetric. VERIFICATION: server decodes header+payload, recomputes signature with its secret/public key, compares. If match, token is valid and untampered. STATELESS: no server-side session storage needed. Server doesn't need to query a database to verify identity. EDGE CASES: JWT can't be revoked before expiry (stateless = no server-side invalidation). FIX: use short expiry (15 min) + refresh tokens (stored server-side, revocable, long-lived). Or maintain a token blacklist in Redis (defeats stateless purpose but adds revocation). Token size: JWTs can grow large (1-4 KB) — stored in every request header. Don't put unnecessary data in the payload.

Standard for third-party authorization (Login with Google). Flow: (1) User clicks 'Login with Google' → redirect to Google's auth server with client_id + redirect_uri. (2) User authenticates on Google → Google redirects back to your app with an authorization_code. (3) Your BACKEND exchanges code + client_secret with Google's token endpoint → receives access_token + refresh_token. (4) Use access_token to call Google APIs on behalf of the user. PKCE extension (required for mobile/SPA): no client_secret. Instead, generate code_verifier (random string), send code_challenge = SHA256(code_verifier) in step 1. In step 3, send code_verifier — Google verifies it matches the challenge. Prevents authorization code interception attacks.

In Transit: TLS (HTTPS) encrypts all data between client and server. Use mTLS (mutual TLS) for service-to-service communication inside the cluster — both sides present certificates. At Rest: AES-256-GCM encryption for data stored on disk. Key management: use a KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) — application never handles raw encryption keys. Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts a data encryption key (DEK) → DEK encrypts the data → store encrypted DEK alongside encrypted data.

Traditional security: trust everything inside the network perimeter (VPN). Zero Trust: never trust, always verify. Every request must be authenticated and authorized, even between internal services. Implementation: mTLS between all services (Istio service mesh), per-request authorization (check JWT + RBAC on every API call), micro-segmentation (network policies limiting which services can talk to which), short-lived credentials (rotate certificates every 24 hours).

Incrementally migrate from a monolith to microservices. Place a facade (API Gateway) in front of the monolith. Gradually route endpoints from the monolith to new microservices. Old code is 'strangled' (replaced) one route at a time. At the end, the monolith is fully replaced. WHY: avoids the risk of a Big Bang rewrite. You can validate each microservice in production before moving the next endpoint. CONFIGURABLE: use feature flags or traffic splitting (route 10% of /orders to new service, 90% to monolith).

Deploy a helper process alongside the main application container (in the same pod in Kubernetes). The sidecar handles cross-cutting concerns: logging (Fluentd sidecar ships logs), monitoring (Prometheus sider), security (Envoy sidecar handles mTLS), traffic management (Istio sidecar proxies all network traffic). The main application is unaware of the sidecar — they communicate via localhost.

When integrating with a legacy system or third-party API that has a different domain model, add a translation layer. Your services communicate with the ACL, which translates between your clean domain model and the legacy model. Prevents legacy concepts from leaking into your codebase.

chapters.title: Algorithms & Data Structures for System Design
chapters.summary: Probabilistic data structures (Bloom filter, Count-Min Sketch, HyperLogLog), spatial data structures (Quadtree, GeoHash, R-tree), and algorithmic building blocks used in large-scale systems.

explanation.overview: Certain algorithmic building blocks appear repeatedly in system design. Bloom filters tell you if an element is NOT in a set (with zero false negatives). HyperLogLog counts unique elements in constant memory. Quadtrees and GeoHashes enable proximity search. Understanding these gives you powerful tools for interviews.

key_concepts.definition: Space-efficient probabilistic set membership test. Answers 'is X in the set?' with two possible results: DEFINITELY NOT (100% accurate) or PROBABLY YES (false positive possible). INTERNAL: a bit array of m bits (all 0 initially) + k independent hash functions. INSERT(x): compute k hashes → set bits at those k positions to 1. LOOKUP(x): compute k hashes → check if ALL k positions are 1. If any is 0, x is DEFINITELY NOT in the set. If all are 1, x is PROBABLY in the set (could be a collision). FALSE POSITIVE RATE: p ≈ (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. For 1% false positive rate with 1M elements: m ≈ 9.6M bits (1.2 MB), k ≈ 7 hash functions. CANNOT DELETE elements (setting a bit to 0 affects other elements that hash to the same bit). FIX: Counting Bloom Filter (each position is a counter instead of a bit — increment on insert, decrement on delete). USE CASES: (1) Chrome Safe Browsing: checks URLs against a Bloom filter of known malicious URLs before querying the server. (2) Cassandra/HBase: checks if an SSTable might contain a key before reading from disk. (3) Spell checkers: check if a word is NOT in the dictionary. (4) Weak password check: check if password is in the list of compromised passwords.

Probabilistic frequency counter. Estimates how many times an element has been seen. Uses a 2D array (d rows × w columns) + d hash functions. INCREMENT(x): for each hash function i, increment array[i][hash_i(x) % w]. ESTIMATE(x): return min(array[i][hash_i(x) % w]) for all i. Always OVERESTIMATES (never underestimates). Accuracy improves with larger d and w. USE: (1) Network traffic frequency estimation (count packets per IP). (2) Top-K heavy hitters (find most frequent search queries). (3) Live stream analytics (approximate word counts).

Estimates cardinality (count of distinct elements) in O(1) memory. Counting unique visitors to a website: with a set, you'd need memory proportional to the number of unique visitors. HLL uses ~12 KB of memory to count up to billions of unique elements with < 1% error. INTERNAL: hash each element → look at the binary representation → count the position of the first 1 bit (leading zeros). The intuition: seeing many leading zeros is increasingly rare. If the maximum leading zeros seen is 10, there are approximately 2^10 = 1024 unique elements. To reduce variance, split the hash into m buckets (registers), compute per-bucket estimates, and take the harmonic mean. Redis: PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE (merge multiple HLLs = union of sets). USE CASES: (1) Unique visitor counting (Redis HLL). (2) Google BigQuery approximate_count_distinct(). (3) Network monitoring (unique IP counts).

configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Tuning configuration to drop stale packets reduces latency but requires robust frontend exception handling.

key_concepts.definition: Encode a (latitude, longitude) pair into a string by alternating bit representation of latitude and longitude ranges, then base32 encoding. 'dpz83' represents a rectangular area. Longer strings = smaller area = more precision. 4 characters ≈ 40×20 km. 6 characters ≈ 600×600 m. 8 characters ≈ 20×20 m. KEY PROPERTY: geohashes with a common prefix are geographically close. So proximity search = prefix match query (efficient with B-Tree index). EDGE CASE: boundary problem — two nearby points on opposite sides of a boundary have entirely different geohashes. FIX: search the 8 neighboring geohash cells too. USED BY: Elasticsearch geo_point, Redis GEOADD (uses sorted set with geohash as score).

Recursively divide a 2D space into 4 quadrants. Each node has 4 children (NW, NE, SW, SE). A leaf node contains up to K points. When a leaf exceeds K, split into 4 children and redistribute points. SEARCH (find points within a rectangle): start at root, for each child check if the child's bounding box intersects the search rectangle, recursively search intersecting children. TIME: O(log N) for well-distributed points. USED BY: Uber for finding nearby drivers. Yelp for nearby restaurants. Game engines for spatial indexing. CONFIGURABLE: max depth, max points per leaf, dynamic rebalancing.

Similar to B-Tree but for multi-dimensional data. Each node contains a bounding rectangle that encompasses all its children. Used by PostGIS (Postgres spatial extension) for spatial queries. Supports: point-in-polygon, nearest-neighbor, range queries. More general than Quadtree — works with arbitrary rectangles and polygons, not just points.

examples.title: Uber's Geospatial Architecture: From Quadtrees to H3
examples.description: How Uber scales location matching for millions of drivers and riders using hexagonal hierarchical spatial indexing.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Uber needs to instantly match a rider with the nearest 5 drivers. Calculating the Haversine distance (great-circle distance) between the rider and every single 100,000 active drivers in a city requires enormous CPU overhead.

The Evolution:
1. Early Days (Quadtrees): Uber initially used Quadtrees to segment the map into squares. A quadtree node would split when it held too many drivers. To find drivers, Uber queried the quadtree node containing the rider.
2. The Flaw with Squares: Bounding boxes are squares. Searching 'within a radius' on a square grid means the diagonal corners are further away than the edges, causing inaccurate distance sorting.
3. The Innovation (H3): Uber invented H3, an open-source Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index. Hexagons are the closest shape to a circle that can seamlessly tile a flat plane. 

The Architecture:
When a driver pings their GPS location, Uber's backend calculates the H3 Hexagon ID for that lat/long. It stores the driver in a Redis cluster keyed by the Hexagon ID. When a rider opens the app, Uber calculates the rider's Hexagon ID and fetches all drivers in that hexagon (and the 6 immediately adjacent hexagons) from Redis in O(1) time.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Never calculate distances against raw coordinates in a database (e.g., `SELECT * WHERE distance(lat, lon) < 5`). Always use a spatial index (Geohash, Quadtree, H3) to map 2D coordinates into a 1D string/integer, allowing O(1) lookups in standard K-V stores or B-Trees.

examples.title: Spatial Data Structure Decision Matrix
examples.description: Use this matrix to justify your geospatial architecture in systems like Uber, Yelp, or Tinder.
examples.code:
ARCHITECTURE                   | INTERNAL MECHANISM           | ACCURACY | BEST USED FOR
-------------------------------|------------------------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------
PostGIS (R-Tree)               | Tree of Bounding Boxes       | Perfect  | Complex polygons, traditional GIS, exact boundaries
Geohash (Elasticsearch/Redis)  | Z-Order Curve (Base32 String)| Low-Med  | "Points of interest within X miles" (Yelp, Tinder)
Quadtree                       | Splitting Squares            | Medium   | Dynamic densities (dense cities vs sparse rural)
H3 (Hexagonal Grid)            | Hexagons with identical radii| High     | Distance-critical sweeping algorithms (Uber, Lyft)

key_concepts.definition: Binary tree of hashes. Leaf nodes = hash(data chunk). Parent nodes = hash(left_child + right_child). Root hash summarizes ALL data. If any chunk changes, the root hash changes. COMPARISON: to find which chunks differ between two replicas: compare root hashes. If different, compare children recursively. Only need to exchange O(log N) hashes to find the differing chunk. USED BY: Cassandra (anti-entropy repair — find inconsistent data between replicas), Git (each commit is a Merkle tree of files), BitTorrent (verify downloaded pieces), Bitcoin (Merkle root in block header).

Tree where each edge represents a character. A path from root to a node represents a prefix. Each node stores whether it marks the end of a complete word/key. LOOKUP/INSERT: O(L) where L = key length (independent of N, number of keys). USE CASES: autocomplete (traverse to the prefix node, DFS to find all completions), IP routing (longest prefix matching), spell checking, phone contact search. COMPRESSED TRIE (Radix Tree): merge single-child chains. Reduces height and memory. Used by Linux kernel for routing tables.

Probabilistic sorted linked list with multiple levels. Bottom level = complete sorted list. Each higher level is a random subset (each element promoted with probability 1/2). SEARCH: start at top level, move right until next element > target, drop down a level, repeat. Average O(log N). INSERT: insert in bottom level, flip a coin to decide promotion to each higher level. WHY: achieves O(log N) search/insert like a balanced tree but much simpler to implement, especially for concurrent access (no tree rotations). USED BY: Redis sorted sets (ZSET), LevelDB/RocksDB memtable.

chapters.title: Service Discovery, Containers & Orchestration
chapters.summary: Container internals (namespaces, cgroups), Kubernetes architecture (kube-apiserver, etcd, kubelet, scheduler), service discovery mechanisms, and service mesh (Istio/Envoy).

explanation.overview: Modern distributed systems run as containers orchestrated by Kubernetes. Understanding how containers work internally, how Kubernetes schedules and manages them, and how services find each other (service discovery) is essential for designing real production systems.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: A container is NOT a lightweight VM. It's a regular Linux process isolated using two kernel features: (1) Namespaces: isolate what the process can SEE. PID namespace: process sees only its own processes (PID 1 inside container). Network namespace: process gets its own network stack (virtual NIC, IP, port space). Mount namespace: process has its own filesystem view. User namespace: UID 0 inside container ≠ UID 0 on host (rootless containers). (2) cgroups (Control Groups): limit what the process can USE. CPU: cpu.max (e.g., 200000 100000 = 2 CPU cores). Memory: memory.max (512 MB hard limit — exceeded = OOM kill). I/O: io.max (bandwidth and IOPS limits). Together: the process thinks it has its own isolated machine, but it's actually sharing the host kernel.

A Docker image is a stack of read-only layers. Each Dockerfile instruction (FROM, RUN, COPY) creates a new layer. Layers are cached and shared between images. A running container adds a writable layer on top (Copy-on-Write — when a file from a read-only layer is modified, it's copied to the writable layer). UNION FILESYSTEM: overlay2 (Linux default) stacks layers into a single coherent filesystem. IMAGE SIZE OPTIMIZATION: use multi-stage builds (build in a large image, copy binary to a tiny alpine image). Minimize layers (combine RUN commands). Use .dockerignore. Base image matters: node:18 (900 MB) vs node:18-alpine (100 MB).

VM: runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor. Each VM has its own kernel — complete isolation. Boot time: 30-60 seconds. Overhead: 200-500 MB per VM. Container: shares the host kernel. Isolation via namespaces/cgroups — lighter but less isolated than VMs. Boot time: < 1 second. Overhead: < 10 MB. Trade-off: VMs for multi-tenant isolation (cloud providers isolate customers with VMs). Containers for microservice deployment (same trust boundary, shared kernel). AWS Firecracker: micro-VMs — VM-level isolation with container-like speed (boot in 125ms). Used by AWS Lambda and Fargate.

examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

key_concepts.definition: kube-apiserver: REST API server (the front door to K8s). All commands (kubectl, CI/CD, controllers) go through the API server. Validates requests, persists state to etcd, and notifies controllers. etcd: distributed key-value store (Raft consensus). Stores ALL cluster state: pods, services, config maps, secrets. The single source of truth. kube-scheduler: watches for unscheduled pods, selects the best node based on: resource requests (CPU, memory), affinity/anti-affinity rules, taints/tolerations, topology spread constraints. Scheduling is a 2-phase process: filtering (eliminate unsuitable nodes) → scoring (rank remaining nodes). kube-controller-manager: runs control loops (reconciliation loops). Deployment controller: ensures desired replica count. ReplicaSet controller: creates/deletes pods to match desired count. Service controller: manages cloud load balancers. cloud-controller-manager: integrates with cloud APIs (AWS, GCP) for load balancers, volumes, routes.

kubelet: agent on each node. Watches the API server for pods assigned to its node, ensures containers are running (pulls images, starts containers, monitors health, reports status back to API server). Restarts containers on failure. kube-proxy: maintains network rules on each node. Implements Service (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) by programming iptables or IPVS rules. When you create a Service, kube-proxy updates iptables on every node so that traffic to the Service's virtual IP is forwarded to one of the backend pod IPs. Container Runtime: actually runs containers. containerd (Docker's runtime, now standalone), CRI-O (lightweight K8s-focused runtime). K8s talks to runtime via CRI (Container Runtime Interface).

the smallest deployable unit. One or more co-located containers sharing the same network namespace (same IP, same port space, can communicate via localhost) and storage volumes. WHY multiple containers? Sidecar pattern: main app container + log collector sidecar + Envoy proxy sidecar. LIFECYCLE: Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed. Init containers run first (database migrations, config fetching). Probes: livenessProbe (is container alive? If not, restart it), readinessProbe (is container ready to serve traffic? If not, remove from Service endpoints), startupProbe (for slow-starting apps, prevents liveness from killing during startup).

In Kubernetes, every Service gets a DNS name: my-service.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local. CoreDNS (runs as a pod) resolves this to the Service's ClusterIP. kube-proxy routes ClusterIP to backend pod IPs. Zero application change needed — just use the DNS name. HEADLESS SERVICE (clusterIP: None): returns pod IPs directly instead of a ClusterIP. Used when you need to connect to specific pods (stateful workloads like Cassandra — each pod has a unique identity).

The client queries a service registry (Consul, Eureka, etcd) to get a list of available service instances, then load-balances among them. Client decides which instance to call. PROS: no single-point-of-failure load balancer, client can use smart routing (same-zone affinity). CONS: client must implement discovery logic for every language. Netflix Eureka + Ribbon (Java) was the canonical example.

The client sends requests to a load balancer/reverse proxy, which queries the service registry and routes to a healthy instance. Client only knows the LB address. PROS: client is simple. CONS: LB is a potential bottleneck/SPOF. This is the Kubernetes model (kube-proxy acts as the server-side discovery).

Deploy a sidecar proxy (Envoy) alongside every service pod. All network traffic goes through the sidecar. The mesh provides: mTLS (automatic encryption between services), traffic management (canary deployments — route 5% to v2, 95% to v1), observability (distributed tracing, request metrics per service-pair), circuit breaking, retries, timeout — ALL without changing application code. CONTROL PLANE (Istiod): configures all sidecar proxies centrally. Creates routing rules, distributes certificates, collects telemetry. DATA PLANE: Envoy sidecars intercept all traffic. OVERHEAD: ~2-5ms latency per hop, ~50 MB memory per sidecar. WHEN TO USE: large microservice architectures (>20 services) where cross-cutting concerns (security, observability, traffic management) are too complex to implement in each service.

examples.title: Netflix Architecture: From Eureka to Envoy
examples.description: The evolution of service discovery at Netflix, from client-side Java libraries (Eureka) to a language-agnostic Service Mesh (Envoy).
examples.code:
The Past (Client-Side Discovery):
In the early 2010s, Netflix built 'Eureka' (Service Registry) and 'Ribbon' (Client-side Load Balancer). When a Java microservice booted up, it registered its IP with Eureka. When Service A wanted to call Service B, Service A's Ribbon library fetched the list of Service B's IPs from Eureka and picked one using Round Robin. This was revolutionary, but it required every microservice to run the JVM and include complex Netflix jar files.

The Present (Service Mesh with Envoy):
As Netflix adopted Node.js, Python, and Go, maintaining client-side libraries in every language became impossible. They transitioned to a Service Mesh. Today, a C++ sidecar proxy called 'Envoy' runs next to every microservice container. 

How it works now:
If the Python 'RecommendationService' wants to call the Java 'UserService', it simply makes a standard local HTTP call to `http://localhost:8080/users`. The Envoy sidecar intercepts this localhost call, looks up the destination in the central control plane, handles mTLS encryption, performs retries, and routes the traffic to a healthy UserService instance over the network. The Python app is completely unaware of the network topology.

examples.title: Service Discovery Registry Implementation (Python + Redis)
examples.description: A conceptual snippet showing how services register themselves via heartbeats using Redis expiration keys.
examples.code:
import redis
import time
import threading

class ServiceRegistry:
    def __init__(self, redis_host='localhost'):
        self.r = redis.Redis(host=redis_host, decode_responses=True)
    
    def register_service(self, service_name, instance_ip, ttl_seconds=10):
        # 1. Register the instance with a TTL.
        # If the instance crashes and stops heartbeating, Redis auto-deletes it.
        key = f"service:{service_name}:{instance_ip}"
        self.r.setex(key, ttl_seconds, "ALIVE")
        
        # 2. Add to a set so we can find all IPs for a service
        self.r.sadd(f"discovery:{service_name}", instance_ip)

    def get_healthy_instances(self, service_name):
        # 1. Get all registered IPs for this service
        ips = self.r.smembers(f"discovery:{service_name}")
        
        healthy_ips = []
        for ip in ips:
            # 2. Check if the heartbeat key still exists
            if self.r.exists(f"service:{service_name}:{ip}"):
                healthy_ips.append(ip)
            else:
                # 3. Clean up dead instances
                self.r.srem(f"discovery:{service_name}", ip)
                
        return healthy_ips

# Usage in a background thread of a microservice:
# def heartbeat():
#     while True:
#         registry.register_service("payment-api", "10.0.1.45")
#         time.sleep(5)  # Send heartbeat every 5 seconds

examples.title: API Gateway vs Service Mesh Decision Matrix
examples.description: Clarify the boundaries between North-South (Gateway) and East-West (Mesh) traffic management.
examples.code:
FEATURE                          | API GATEWAY (e.g., AWS API Gateway) | SERVICE MESH (e.g., Istio / Envoy) 
---------------------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------
Traffic Direction                | North-South (Client to Cluster)   | East-West (Service to Service)
Primary Purpose                  | Aggregation, Auth, Rate Limiting  | mTLS, Retries, Circuit Breaking, Tracing
Knows about User Sessions?       | Yes (Validates external JWTs)     | No (Usually deals with internal IAM)
Deployment Model                 | Centralized Cluster at Edge       | Distributed Sidecars per Pod
Protocol Support                 | Mostly HTTP / REST / GraphQL      | HTTP, gRPC, TCP, Redis, Mongo
Do you need both?                | YES. They serve different layers. | YES. Gateways handle edge, Mesh handles internal.

chapters.title: DevOps, CI/CD & Observability
chapters.summary: CI/CD pipeline design, the three pillars of observability (metrics, logs, traces), monitoring best practices, alerting strategies, and SRE concepts.

explanation.overview: DevOps bridges development and operations — ensuring code is deployed safely, frequently, and automatically. Observability ensures you can understand what's happening inside your production system by examining its external outputs. In system design interviews, you're expected to know how the system is deployed and monitored.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Every commit triggers: code checkout → build → lint → unit tests → integration tests → artifact creation (Docker image, JAR). Fast feedback: developers know within 5-10 minutes if their change broke anything. BEST PRACTICES: (1) Run tests in parallel (split across pods). (2) Cache dependencies (node_modules, Maven .m2). (3) Fail fast (lint first, then unit tests, then slow integration tests). (4) Trunk-based development (short-lived branches, merge to main daily). TOOLS: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI, ArgoCD.

Continuous Delivery: after CI passes, the artifact is READY to deploy (manual approval before production). Continuous Deployment: after CI passes, the artifact is AUTOMATICALLY deployed to production (no human approval). Most organizations do Continuous Delivery with automated staging deploy + manual production approval.

Rolling Update (K8s default): replace old pods one at a time with new pods. minAvailable ensures minimum capacity during deploy. Zero downtime but both versions coexist during rollout — APIs must be backward compatible. Blue-Green: two identical environments (Blue = current, Green = new). Deploy to Green, test, then switch traffic (DNS or LB). Instant rollback (switch back to Blue). COST: 2× infrastructure during deploy. Canary: route 1-5% of traffic to new version. Monitor error rate, latency, business metrics. If OK, gradually increase (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%). If problems, rollback immediately. A/B Testing: like canary but based on user segments (new users, specific region, premium tier) for feature evaluation, not just safety.

examples.title: Netflix Spinnaker & Automated Canary Analysis (ACA)
examples.description: How Netflix safely deploys thousands of times a day without human manual testing using statistical canary analysis.
examples.code:
The Problem:
Deploying to 100% of servers at once causes catastrophic global outages if a bug slips through CI. Manual canary deployments (deploying to 1 server and having a human watch the logs) doesn't scale for 1000s of microservices.

The Architecture (Spinnaker + Kayenta):
Netflix open-sourced Spinnaker, their continuous delivery platform. When a developer merges code, Spinnaker starts an 'Automated Canary Deployment'.
1. It spins up three clusters: Production (existing), Baseline (a fresh copy of the old code), and Canary (the new code). *Why Baseline? Because a brand new cold-started pod behaves differently than a pod that has been running for 5 days. Comparing Canary to Baseline ensures an apples-to-apples comparison.
2. It routes 1% of traffic to Baseline and 1% to Canary.
3. Kayenta (the ACA engine) pulls 1,000+ metrics (CPU, memory, HTTP 500s, p99 latency) from both clusters for 30 minutes.
4. It performs statistical T-tests on the metrics. If the Canary deviates negatively from the Baseline by more than a threshold, Spinnaker automatically kills the Canary and aborts the deploy. If it passes, it rolls out to 100%.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Continuous Deployment at scale relies entirely on observability. You cannot do CD without phenomenal, automated metric collection and alerting. Human validation does not scale.

examples.title: Deployment Strategy Matrix
examples.description: Choose the correct deployment rollout strategy in an interview scenario based on risk tolerance and system state.
examples.code:
STRATEGY             | DOWNTIME | ROLLBACK SPEED | COST THOUGH DEPLOY | BEST USED FOR
---------------------|----------|----------------|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------
Recreate             | High     | Very Slow      | Normal             | Stateful legacy systems, Dev environments
Rolling Update       | Zero     | Slow           | Normal             | General microservices (Default K8s behavior)
Blue/Green           | Zero     | Instant        | 2x Normal          | Critical high-traffic services, DB schema changes done carefully
Canary               | Zero     | Fast           | Normal             | Extreme scale (FAANG), risky algorithm changes
A/B Testing          | Zero     | N/A            | Normal             | Product validation (testing if a new button color increases sales)

configurable_params.name: Library Configuration Parameters
configurable_params.default: Default library settings usually favor CP over AP
configurable_params.effect: You can modify connection timeouts, retry buffers, and max memory limits.

key_concepts.definition: Numeric measurements collected at regular intervals. Types: Counter (monotonically increasing — total requests, total errors), Gauge (point-in-time value — current CPU %, memory usage, active connections), Histogram (distribution of values — request latency split into buckets: <10ms, <50ms, <100ms, <500ms). USE p99 latency, not average (average hides outliers — 99 requests at 10ms + 1 at 10s = average 109ms masks the 10s request). RED Method (rate, errors, duration) for request-driven services. USE Method (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources (CPU, memory, disk). TOOLS: Prometheus (pull-based metric collection, stores time series), Grafana (dashboards), Datadog, CloudWatch. PROMETHEUS INTERNAL: Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints every 15-60 seconds. Data stored as time series: metric_name{label=value} → [(timestamp, value), ...]. PromQL query language: http_requests_total{method='GET', status=~'5..'}. rate() computes per-second rate. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...) computes p99 latency.

Timestamped, unstructured or structured text recording events. STRUCTURED LOGGING: use JSON format — {timestamp, level, service, trace_id, user_id, message, ...}. Enables efficient search and aggregation. NEVER log: passwords, tokens, PII (personal data — GDPR compliance). LEVELS: DEBUG (development only), INFO (normal operations), WARN (unexpected but recovered), ERROR (failure requiring attention). LOG PIPELINE: Application → Fluentd/Filebeat (collect) → Kafka (buffer) → Elasticsearch (store + index) → Kibana (search + visualize). This is the ELK/EFK stack. Elasticsearch inverted index enables full-text search across billions of log lines in milliseconds. LOG RETENTION: 7-30 days hot (Elasticsearch), 90 days warm (cheaper storage), 1 year cold (S3/Glacier for compliance).

Follows a single request across multiple microservices. A trace consists of spans — each span represents one service's processing of the request. Span contains: trace_id (unique per request), span_id, parent_span_id, service name, operation, start time, duration, status, tags. The trace_id is propagated via HTTP headers (traceparent in W3C Trace Context, or X-B3-TraceId in Zipkin format) so every service logs the same trace_id. VISUALIZATION: Jaeger or Zipkin renders a waterfall graph showing how long each service took and the call sequence (Service A → Service B → Service C → Database). USE WHEN: debugging latency (which service is slow?), understanding dependencies (which services are called?), error tracing (which service caused the 500?). TOOLS: Jaeger, Zipkin, AWS X-Ray, Datadog APM. OpenTelemetry: vendor-neutral standard for metrics, logs, and traces — instrument once, send to any backend.

examples.title: SRE Alerting: PromQL for SLA Violation
examples.description: A real-world Prometheus query to trigger a PagerDuty alert when the 99th percentile latency of the checkout API exceeds 500ms.
examples.code:
# Calculate the 99th percentile latency over the last 5 minutes
# for the '/api/v1/checkout' endpoint.
histogram_quantile(
  0.99, 
  sum by (le) (
    rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{path="/api/v1/checkout"}[5m])
  )
) > 0.500

# How SREs use this:
# This query is placed in an Alertmanager rule. If this expression evaluates 
# to TRUE for more than 2 minutes (to ignore 5-second network blips), 
# Alertmanager fires a webhook to PagerDuty, which calls the on-call engineer's phone.

key_concepts.definition: ALERT ON SYMPTOMS, NOT CAUSES. Bad alert: 'CPU > 90%' (CPU could be high during normal batch processing). Good alert: 'p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes' (directly impacts users). Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting: if you're consuming your monthly error budget 10× faster than expected, alert. If 2× faster, warn. PAGES: only page humans for issues requiring immediate action. Use Slack/email for non-urgent. PagerDuty for pages. RUNBOOKS: every alert must link to a runbook — step-by-step instructions to diagnose and resolve the issue. Reduces MTTR.

SLO (Service Level Objective): availability target (99.9% = 8.76 hours downtime/year). Error Budget = 100% - SLO = 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month of acceptable downtime. IF error budget remaining: deploy fast, take risks. IF error budget exhausted: freeze deployments, focus on reliability. This creates a quantitative framework for balancing feature velocity and reliability. Google SRE: the team that invented this practice.

chapters.title: Disaster Recovery, Backup & Data Integrity
chapters.summary: Disaster recovery planning (RPO/RTO), backup strategies, multi-region architecture, data migration, data integrity verification, and incident response.

explanation.overview: Disasters happen: datacenter fires, region-wide outages, ransomware attacks, accidental data deletion, database corruption. Disaster Recovery (DR) planning ensures your system can recover from these events within acceptable time (RTO) and data loss (RPO) bounds. This is the ultimate test of system design — everything you build must survive the worst-case scenario.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. RPO = 0: no data loss (synchronous replication to standby). RPO = 1 hour: can lose up to 1 hour of data (hourly backups or near-sync replication). RPO = 24 hours: can lose up to a day (daily backups). COST: lower RPO = more expensive (synchronous replication costs throughput and latency). RPO directly determines your backup/replication frequency.

Maximum acceptable downtime. RTO = 0: no downtime (active-active multi-region). RTO = 15 minutes: failover to hot standby. RTO = 4 hours: restore from backup to warm standby. RTO = 24 hours: rebuild from backups. COST: lower RTO = more expensive (maintaining hot standby infrastructure that's idle during normal operation).

Backup & Restore (RPO: hours, RTO: hours): take periodic backups to S3/GCS. On disaster, provision new infrastructure and restore from backups. Cheapest but slowest recovery. Pilot Light (RPO: minutes, RTO: minutes-hours): core infrastructure always running in DR region (database replication, basic networking). On disaster, scale up compute (start app servers, scale ASG). Warm Standby (RPO: seconds, RTO: minutes): fully running DR region at reduced capacity (fewer instances). On disaster, scale to full capacity and redirect traffic. Hot Standby / Active-Active (RPO: 0, RTO: ~0): both regions actively serving traffic. Data replicated synchronously or near-synchronously. On disaster, the surviving region handles all traffic. Most expensive but zero data loss and near-zero downtime. USED BY: banks (hot standby for core banking), large e-commerce (active-active for zero downtime).

examples.title: Disaster Recovery Strategy Decision Matrix
examples.description: Evaluate the optimal DR plan based on business cost tolerance and downtime requirements.
examples.code:
DR PATTERN                   | INFRA DEV/MAINT COST | RECOVERY POINT (RPO) | RECOVERY TIME (RTO) | BEST USED FOR
-----------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------
Backup and Restore           | $ (Lowest)            | 1-24 Hours           | 4-24 Hours          | Non-critical internal apps, batch analytics jobs
Pilot Light                  | $$                    | 10-60 Mins           | 1-4 Hours           | Standard web applications, read-heavy sites
Warm Standby                 | $$$                   | 0-5 Mins             | 10-60 Mins          | Business-critical B2B SaaS, standard e-commerce
Multi-Region Active-Active   | $$$$$ (Highest)       | Zero (0s)            | Near Zero (<1 min)  | FAANG, Global Payments, Heartbeat monitors

key_concepts.definition: Full Backup: complete copy of all data. Simple to restore (just load the full backup). Expensive in storage and time. Typically run weekly. Incremental Backup: only data changed since the LAST backup (full or incremental). Small and fast. Restore requires: full backup + all incremental backups in order. If any incremental is corrupted, all subsequent backups are unusable. Typically run daily or hourly. Differential Backup: only data changed since the LAST FULL backup. Larger than incremental (accumulates over time) but easier to restore (full + latest differential). Snapshot (Database/Storage level): point-in-time copy using Copy-on-Write. Near-instantaneous (only metadata is copied; data pages are shared). When original data is modified, the old page is preserved (CoW). Used by: EBS snapshots, ZFS snapshots, LVM snapshots, RDS automated snapshots.

3 copies of data (1 primary + 2 backups). 2 different storage types (SSD + tape, or EBS + S3). 1 offsite copy (different region/cloud provider). This protects against: hardware failure (copy 2), facility disaster (offsite copy), and ransomware (if attacker encrypts primary + first backup, offsite is safe). IMMUTABLE BACKUPS: S3 Object Lock (WORM — Write Once Read Many) prevents anyone from deleting/modifying backups for a retention period. Critical for ransomware protection.

A backup is worthless if you can't restore from it. REGULARLY test: full restore to a separate environment, verify data integrity (checksums), measure actual restore time (does it meet your RTO?). Chaos engineering for backups: once a quarter, simulate a disaster and restore from backups. If you haven't tested your backups, you don't have backups — you have hope.

Every data write includes a checksum (CRC32, SHA-256). On read, recompute the checksum and compare. If mismatch → data corruption detected (bit rot, disk failure, bug). S3: Content-MD5 header for upload verification. PostgreSQL: data page checksums (data_checksums = on — detects page-level corruption). ZFS: checksums every block with automatic repair from redundant copies.

Periodic background processes that compare data from two sources and fix discrepancies. Example: compare order count in Order Service DB vs count of payment records in Payment Service DB. If mismatch, flag for investigation. IMPLEMENTATION: nightly cron job that: (1) queries source A for all records in date range, (2) queries source B for matching records, (3) identifies mismatches (missing, extra, or differing records), (4) stores discrepancies in a reconciliation report, (5) optionally auto-corrects (if trusted source is clear). USED BY: financial systems (bank balance reconciliation), e-commerce (inventory audit), data pipelines (row count verification between source and destination).

Append-only log of all critical operations: who did what, when, from where. Never modified or deleted. Store in a tamper-proof location (S3 with Object Lock, append-only database table with no DELETE/UPDATE permissions). Required for: financial compliance (SOX), healthcare (HIPAA), any system where accountability matters. IMPLEMENTATION: every API call that modifies data writes to an audit log: {timestamp, user_id, action, resource, old_value, new_value, ip_address, result}.

examples.title: End-to-End Data Integrity: Python SHA-256 Verification
examples.description: A functional snippet showing how to verify data integrity before relying on it (e.g., downloading an S3 Backup).
examples.code:
import hashlib
import os

def generate_checksum(filepath):
    """Generates a SHA-256 checksum for a large file in chunks to save memory."""
    sha256_hash = hashlib.sha256()
    # Read file in 4MB chunks
    with open(filepath, "rb") as f:
        for byte_block in iter(lambda: f.read(4096 * 1024), b""):
            sha256_hash.update(byte_block)
    return sha256_hash.hexdigest()

def verify_backup_integrity(backup_filepath, original_checksum):
    """Simulates restoring a backup and verifying it hasn't suffered bit-rot."""
    if not os.path.exists(backup_filepath):
        raise FileNotFoundError("Backup file missing!")
        
    print("Calculating checksum of restored backup...")
    restored_checksum = generate_checksum(backup_filepath)
    
    if restored_checksum == original_checksum:
        print("[SUCCESS] Integrity Verified! Checksum matches.")
        return True
    else:
        print(f"[FATAL] Corruption Detected!\nExpected: {original_checksum}\nGot: {restored_checksum}")
        # Trigger immediate alert. NEVER restore this backup to production.
        return False

# Usage in a Cron Job:
# verify_backup_integrity('/mnt/backups/db_dump_2024.sql', 'e3b0c442...')

key_concepts.definition: Primary region handles all traffic. Secondary region receives replicated data (async) and is on standby. On primary failure, DNS failover routes traffic to secondary. RTO: minutes (DNS propagation + failover). RPO: seconds (replication lag). CHEAPER than active-active. Suitable when a few minutes of downtime is acceptable.

Both regions serve traffic simultaneously. Data replicated bi-directionally. RTO ≈ 0 (no failover needed — surviving region handles all traffic). RPO ≈ 0 (synchronous or near-synchronous replication). CHALLENGES: write conflicts (two regions modify same record). Resolution: LWW (Last Writer Wins — risk data loss), CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types — merge operations mathematically), application-level merge (domain-specific logic). USED BY: Google Spanner (globally consistent via TrueTime), CockroachDB (multi-region with serializable isolation), Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables (active-active with LWW). DESIGN TIP: partition data by user region (US users write to US, EU users write to EU). Most writes are region-local → minimal conflicts. Cross-region reads for data from other regions.

Dual-Write: write to both old and new systems simultaneously. DANGEROUS: no atomicity guarantee — one write can succeed while the other fails. Prefer CDC. Change Data Capture (CDC): Debezium captures every write from the old DB and streams to the new DB via Kafka. Once new DB is fully synced, cut over. Safest approach — keeps both systems in sync. Shadow Reads: after migration, read from both old and new systems, compare results. If they match, the new system is correct. If not, investigate discrepancies before cutover.

examples.title: Netflix Global Active-Active & Multi-Region Evacuation
examples.description: How Netflix routes traffic globally and dynamically evacuates an entire AWS region (e.g., us-east-1) in under 7 minutes during an outage without dropping user streams.
examples.code:
The Architecture:
Netflix runs entirely on AWS across three regions: us-east-1 (N. Virginia), us-west-2 (Oregon), and eu-west-1 (Ireland). The architecture is 'Active-Active'. Every region is capable of serving 100% of the customer base if necessary.

Global State:
To make this possible, heavily mutated data (e.g., user profiles, continuous viewing histories) is stored in Cassandra, using its native multi-region asynchronous replication. When a user watches a movie in New York (us-east-1), the fact that they paused at 32:01 is replicated to Europe and Oregon within milliseconds.

The Evacuation Process:
When internal telemetry detects an anomaly in us-east-1 (elevated error rates, EC2 instance drops), the Netflix SRE team hits a literal 'Evacuate' button. 
1. DNS Routing: AWS Route 53 global DNS records are updated. Traffic from the East Coast USA is instantly rerouted to us-west-2 (Oregon).
2. Auto-Scaling: The microservices in us-west-2 detect the massive traffic spike and trigger aggressive EC2 auto-scaling to absorb the load.
3. Cache Warming: Because Memcached is regional, the cache in Oregon is cold for East Coast users. To prevent DB thrashing during evacuation, Netflix built 'Hollow', an in-memory dataset replication tool that keeps caches warm globally.

Takeaway: 
Achieving an RTO of < 7 minutes for a region-wide cloud outage requires relentless chaos testing. Netflix conducts these evacuations *routinely* (at least once a month) during peak business hours to verify it works.

chapters.title: Case Study: Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL)
chapters.summary: A deep dive into designing a scalable URL shortener like TinyURL or bit.ly, focusing on highly available reads, low latency redirects, and distributed unique ID generation.

explanation.overview: A URL shortener is a classic system design interview question. It tests your ability to translate simple functional requirements ('given a long URL, return a short one') into a distributed system that handles massive read-heavy traffic, predictable storage growth, and collision-free ID generation. The system involves an API gateway, a distributed key-value store or RDBMS, a caching layer, and an offline ID generation service.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: INTERNAL Mechanics: The system fundamentally acts as a massive hash map. When a user submits a long URL, we assign it a unique auto-incrementing integer ID. We convert this integer to Base62 (A-Z, a-z, 0-9) to create a short 7-character string. For example, ID 125 transforms to 'cb'. The short URL is returned. When a user clicks the short URL, the request hits a Load Balancer, checks an in-memory Cache (Redis/Memcached). If there's a cache miss, it hits the primary Database, reconstructs the long URL, caches it, and returns an HTTP 301 or 302 redirect. To ensure scalability, we pre-generate IDs using a dedicated ZooKeeper-backed Key Generation Service (KGS) so Web Servers never block waiting for an ID.

step_by_step.title: Requirements & Estimation
step_by_step.detail: Assume 100M URLs generated per month, 10:1 read-to-write ratio (1B reads/month). At 500 bytes per URL stored for 10 years: 100M * 12 * 10 * 500 = 6TB payload. The scale fits in a standard RDBMS, but NoSQL scales writes easier. 1B reads/mo = ~400 QPS average, ~2K peak QPS. Memory footprint for 20% hot URLs: 200M * 500 bytes = 100GB, easily fitting in a Redis cluster.

step_by_step.title: API Design
step_by_step.detail: POST /api/v1/data/shorten (body: {long_url: string, custom_alias: opt<string>}) -> returns {short_url: string}. GET /api/v1/{short_url} -> throws HTTP 301 (Permanent Redirect - caches long term) or HTTP 302 (Temporary Redirect - allows tracking analytics).

step_by_step.title: Database Schema & Primary Key
step_by_step.detail: Table `url_mapping`: Hash (Base62 string) [PK], Long_URL [Varchar 2048], User_ID, Creation_Date, Expiration_Date. We use a secondary index on Long_URL to prevent duplicate insertions.

step_by_step.title: ID Generation & Base62 Encoding
step_by_step.detail: Using MD5 hash leads to collisions. Using an auto-incrementing DB ID causes write bottlenecks. Instead, a Key Generation Service (KGS) pre-computes Base62 strings and stores them in a DB. Application servers grab a chunk of 1,000 keys into memory. They assign keys instantly without DB locking.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Converting a base-10 integer to base-62 (26 lowercase, 26 uppercase, 10 digits). A 7-character base62 string yields 62^7 = 3.5 trillion unique keys, enough for decades of usage.
301 is Permanent: browser caches the redirect forever, saving server load but destroying analytics tracking. 302 is Temporary: browser hits server every time, higher load, perfect analytics.
A standalone service that pre-computes unique keys and hands them out to web servers in chunks (e.g., 1,000 at a time). This eliminates database contention and network round-trips for ID creation.

limitations: Predictability Hack: If an attacker knows your KGS assigns keys sequentially, they can easily scrape all your URLs. TWEEK/FIX: Add a random shuffling step inside the chunk so keys are distributed non-sequentially.

Custom Aliases: A custom alias ('/mybrand') bypasses the KGS and requires a direct database check for uniqueness, creating a potential race condition. TWEEK: Use an atomic `INSERT IF NOT EXISTS` or Redis exact-lock.

technologies_used.details: A centralized service for maintaining configuration information and naming. Here, it reliably coordinates which chunk of IDs (e.g., 1M to 2M) belongs to which KGS application server, ensuring absolutely zero collisions in distributed environments.

An in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, and message broker. Because URL shortening relies exclusively on random reads for small items (<1KB), Redis provides sub-millisecond lookup times.

A distributed NoSQL database designed to handle large amounts of data across many commodity servers. Ideal for URL shorteners because the data model is a simple Key-Value mapping, and NoSQL excels at massive horizontal write/read scaling without complex JOIN requirements.

chapters.title: Case Study: Distributed Web Crawler (Googlebot)
chapters.summary: Design a highly scalable web crawler capable of downloading and indexing billions of web pages per month while respecting robots.txt and avoiding spider traps.

explanation.overview: A web crawler continuously traverses the internet to download web pages for search engines, archives, or data mining. The core algorithm is a distributed Breadth-First Search (BFS). You start with seed URLs, download the pages, extract links, filter out visited URLs, and add new ones to the queue.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: INTERNAL Mechanics: The system relies on a massively distributed URL Frontier (a priority queue). Worker nodes pull URLs from the Frontier, resolve DNS, fetch HTML, parse it, and extract links. A Bloom Filter checks if a newly found URL has already been visited (we can't use a standard hash set for billions of URLs as it would consume terabytes of RAM). Valid, unvisited links are appended back to the Frontier. The parsed HTML content is streamed to an object store (S3) or BigTable for indexing.

step_by_step.title: URL Frontier Queueing
step_by_step.detail: The Frontier prioritizes URLs based on PageRank, freshness, and domain limits to avoid DDoSing a specific site (politeness).

step_by_step.title: DNS Resolution & Caching
step_by_step.detail: Standard DNS lookups take 10-100ms. A crawler making 10,000 requests/sec will bottleneck hard on DNS. We must use a custom, highly cached DNS resolver.

step_by_step.title: HTML Fetcher & Parser
step_by_step.detail: Fetches the page content. A dedicated parser checks for malicious content, spider traps (infinite dynamic links like `/page/1/page/2`), and extracts out-links.

step_by_step.title: Content Duplication Check (MinHash)
step_by_step.detail: 30% of the web is duplicate content. We use Simhash/MinHash to generate a document fingerprint. If the fingerprint matches an existing one, we discard the page to save storage.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Infinite loops created by dynamic web pages (e.g., recursive calendars). Handled by setting a strict max-depth limit on URLs or using ML algorithms to detect repetitive URL patterns.
Crawlers must never overwhelm a site. The URL Frontier maintains separate queues per domain and ensures a delay (e.g., 5 seconds) between fetches to the same domain.

OPTION Breadth-First (BFS) vs OPTION Depth-First (DFS)
----------------------------------------------------
Pros BFS: Highly parallelizable, naturally finds shortest paths to high-quality domains.
Cons BFS: Requires massive memory for the frontier queue.
Pros DFS: Low memory overhead.
Cons DFS: Easily gets stuck in infinite deep links / spider traps. (Hence BFS is the industry standard).
